## Raster only when pixels are read (2026-11-13)

Step 2 of `docs/perf-goal.md`, lever 1 of `docs/design-review.md`.

### Step 1: what makes pixels in a headless run

- `Page::paint` (headless pixels) has four callers in `bare-drive`: the `shot` step (`run.rs`, after `images_pending`), the failure capture (`run.rs`, only with `--out`), `Page::capture` and `capture_tall`. Nothing else calls it: a frame for `find`, `read`, `click` and `expect` is DOM, style, layout and fragments, with no display list and no raster. `snap.rs` and the hit tests read fragments (`bare_paint::hit`), not pixels. Canvas `getImageData` has its own 2D code in `browser_canvas.rs` and does not use the page raster. Headless raster was lazy already.
- The "paint" share of `curl-se-home` (86.7%), `blog-rust-lang-home` (52.9%) and `rust-lang-org-home` (27.6%) is not `Page::paint`. Frame-pointer stacks from `/data/bare-tmp/prof/cpu/rawfp/` show `Canvas::fill_poly` under `Painter::draw_view`, under `bare_paint::svg::bitmap`, under `images::load`, on an image worker thread. `svg::bitmap` painted each SVG `<img>` file twice (on white and on black) as soon as it arrived, and nobody read the pixels. Inclusive share of `svg::bitmap`: `curl-se-home` 91.1%, `blog-rust-lang-home` 55.7%, `rust-lang-org-home` 54.1%. `Painter::paint` from the page: 0.5%.
- `curl-se-home` has no `shot` step. No driver step decides by pixels (`visible` reads fragments).
- Because the raster ran when a picture arrived, the instruction count of a journey depended on whether the picture arrived before the process ended. Base runs of `curl-se-home` gave 338 to 663 M, and `rust-lang-org-home` 119 M and 280 M.

### Built

- `bare_html::dom::Pixels` replaces `Arc<[u32]>` in `Bitmap`. A vector or an `Arc<[u32]>` makes it at once (`From`). `Pixels::lazy(make)` makes the pixels at the first read (`Deref`, `shared`), once, and clones share them.
- `svg::bitmap_size` gives the size, and the same accept or refuse answer as `svg::bitmap`, without a raster (`parse_file`, then `raster`). `images::load` returns the size and a lazy raster that keeps the file text. The picture budget still reserves `4 * w * h` bytes at load, so a picture that failed before fails now.
- Layout, `naturalWidth`, load and error events read the size only. The display list clones the handle. The raster runs in `Canvas::draw_image` and `Scaled::get`, that is at a screenshot, a window draw or a check frame.
- A second effect: an unread SVG keeps its text (at most 512 KiB), not `4 * w * h` bytes of pixels.

### Numbers (live pages, 3 runs each, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, max RSS, archMachine under load by other agents)

The step-1 corpus is not on main, so these runs use the live sites. BASE `f6415364`, MAIN `a7ba0525`, NEW this branch. Instructions in M, run values.

| Journey | BASE | MAIN | NEW |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `curl-se-home` | 616, 584, 500 | 623, 369, 465 | 106, 106, 106 |
| `blog-rust-lang-home` | 421, 420, 421 | 406, 424, 422 | 186, 187, 188 |
| `rust-lang-org-home` | 119, 118, 118 | 123, 118, 118 | 122, 118, 118 |

Peak RSS (MiB): `curl-se-home` 49, 49, 48 / 40, 37, 37 / 16, 16, 16. `blog-rust-lang-home` 25 to 27 / 27 / 17. `rust-lang-org-home` 17 to 18 on all three: the SVG picture did not arrive before the journey ended in these runs, so the saving is not visible there (an earlier run of BASE took 277 to 280 M when it arrived).

All 48 journeys, 3 runs each (min of 3, without `duckduckgo-html-search`): instructions BASE 25,390 M, MAIN 24,174 M, NEW 24,206 M. RSS sum 1,153 / 1,127 / 1,106 MiB. The total is inside the live noise: other rows move by more than the three rows gain (for example `python-docs-search-results` spreads 2.6 to 2.9 G on one binary, and `python-org-docs-link` and `hn-*` swing on MAIN by load timing). Only `blog-rust-lang-home` and `curl-se-home` show a stable change (-56% and -77% against MAIN). Success criterion 2 (80% of baseline) is not reached by this step.

`duckduckgo-html-search` served a "bots use DuckDuckGo" challenge in some runs (BASE run 3, NEW runs 1 to 3 in the parallel set). A sequential rerun passed on NEW (77 M) and failed once again by challenge. It is a site block, not a result of this change.

### Checks

- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: all pass except 7 TLS tests (`bare-net` `https_openssl` 2, `bare-tls` `client_openssl` 4 and `tls12_openssl` 1). They fail the same way on `a7ba0525` (the openssl on this machine).
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` against `e0fa06eb` (the main this branch sits on): 803 rows, mean change glibc -0.004%, jemalloc +0.000%, no row over the limit. 2 rows do not run on either tree (`examples/parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`, the known stack size issue in the fix candidates above).
- After the rebase: `bare-html`, `bare-paint` and `bare` lib tests pass. `a_slow_fetch_does_not_hold_back_the_requests_queued_after_it` failed once under load and passed alone.
- New tests: `dom::pixels_tests` (made once at the first read, clones share), `svg::file_tests::the_size_alone_agrees_with_the_bitmap`, `images::tests::an_svg_picture_has_its_size_and_no_raster_until_its_pixels_are_read`.
- A local page with two SVG `<img>` (natural size and scaled) and an SVG `background-image`: the `shot` PNG is byte-identical on MAIN and NEW, and `naturalWidth` and `complete` read the right values.
- The tests were written after the code, not before it.

### Not tested

The window mode with a display (only the unit tests that draw into a window buffer, which pass). The corpus runs of step 1. `test262_check.sh` and `exec_diff.sh` (no change in `crates/js`; the change touches `bare_html::dom::Bitmap` only). Cost of the first read of a large SVG inside a window frame (the raster now runs in the frame that needs it, on the main thread, not on a worker).

### Noticed, not changed

- The raster of a lazy SVG now runs on the thread that paints. A window page with a large SVG pays it in one frame; before, a worker paid it. A later step could raster on a worker when the picture enters the viewport.
- `svg::bitmap` parses the file twice when the raster is read (once for the size). A size read of the root tag would avoid the first parse.
- The SVG raster ignores `opacity` on a shape (same on MAIN).

## 2026-11-13: download manager design (proposal)

The owner asked for download handling "like IDM": resume and retry, segmented parallel downloads, a queue with controls. Uploads are out of scope.
`docs/design-downloads.md` holds the design. No code changed.
Measured with `curl`, 3 rounds, n = 1, 4 and 8 range connections, on Wi-Fi from archMachine: more connections did not give a steady gain (best 2.6 times, worst 3.5 times slower). 2 of 6 single-connection runs stalled (0.65 MB/s and 0.08 MB/s). Splitting mainly protects against a stalled connection.
Open owner questions are in section 8 of the design. The first is scope against the login and E2E goal of 2026-11-10.
Owner decision, 2026-11-13: "work it out and get it done". Build all 3 steps now. Pause lasts only while the process runs. `MAX_DOWNLOAD` stays 1 GiB. Start values as in section 8 of the design.

## One network client in `bare-mcp`, and jar-keyed private replies (step 5)

Branch `t3/share-network-client-cache`. Design: `docs/design-suite.md`, section 2 (step 5, design A1) and section 9 (owner decisions 4, 6 and 8). Decision: `docs/decisions.md`, "One network client for `bare-mcp`".

### What was built

- `bare-mcp` keeps one network client in `Server` and gives a fork of it to each `open` (`Session::with_client`, new in `bare-drive`). The connections and the reply cache survive between opens. `Session::new` is unchanged for the step-file runs.
- `open` has a `fresh` parameter (tool schema and description updated). With `fresh: true` the open gets a clean client. The shared one is not touched.
- `bare-net`: a stored reply has an `owner`. `public` and `immutable` replies have owner 0 and answer every jar. Any other reply belongs to the jar that stored it (`Jar::id`, a counter), and it answers that jar only when it is fresh. Another jar asks the server with the validators (`If-None-Match`, `If-Modified-Since`); a 304 gives the stored body. Both lookups (`load`, `hop_stream`) and both stores (`load`, `keep`) use it. The cap and the "empty on overflow" rule did not change.
- Tests (written first, the net one failed before the change): `bare-net` `a_reply_that_is_not_public_answers_only_the_jar_that_stored_it` (stream path and `get`; `private`, plain `max-age`, `public`, `immutable`; a validator case). `bare-mcp` `open_shares_the_http_cache_between_opens_and_fresh_does_not`: two pages of one site, the second open does not fetch the `public` script and does fetch the `private` one, `fresh` fetches again, and a later open is warm again.

### Numbers

Machine archMachine (shared, load 10 to 40). Fixture `/data/bare-tmp/design/suite/server.py` (300 KB script, 60 KB sheet, both `public, immutable`). Driver `mcpdrive.py` (not in the repository): one `bare-mcp` under `perf stat -e instructions:u`; log in once, save the state, then N times `open /pK state=s` and `expect #count`. MAIN is `8eb90c9c`. 3 runs each; run values.

| N opens | build | instructions (M) | peak RSS (MiB) | static requests of the N opens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | MAIN | 983, 982, 983 | 30.2, 30.0, 30.4 | 20, 20, 20 |
| 10 | NEW shared | 981, 980, 983 | 25.4, 25.5, 25.5 | 0, 0, 0 |
| 10 | NEW `fresh` | 983, 984, 982 | 30.4, 30.4, 29.9 | 20, 20, 20 |
| 50 | MAIN | 4115, 4115, 4108 | 37.7, 38.2, 44.2 | 100, 100, 100 |
| 50 | NEW shared | 4110, 4112, 4104 | 25.3, 25.6, 25.9 | 0, 0, 0 |
| 50 | NEW `fresh` | 4117, 4113, 4111 | 37.3, 41.6, 43.0 | 100, 100, 100 |

- The instruction count does not change (0.1%). The reply of a loopback fixture is cheap, and the fetch of a cached script was only 2 of the requests of an open. The gain is the connection and the request on a real network (not measured: the fixture is plain HTTP on loopback).
- **Memory.** The shared client is flat: RSS after 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 opens is 24.3 to 25.9 MiB (setup alone: 23.3 to 23.9 MiB). MAIN and `fresh` grow about 0.3 MiB for each open, and one run reached 44 MiB at 50 opens. The growth stays with a client that is made new for each open, so it is the cost of that client and not of the shared one. Hypothesis (not checked): the worker threads of a dropped client keep their fork, and with it the 64 MiB-capped reply cache of the old client, until the threads park.
- Isolation gate (0.1 MiB for each document): at most 0.04 MiB for each of 50 documents, and flat after 10 opens.
- Warm against cold on the step-file fixture (`cold1.steps` in a new process, `cold10.steps` in one process, 3 runs; the step runner already shared the client): one test in a new process 636, 638, 634 M; 10 tests in one process 5,683, 5,701, 5,705 M (568 to 570 M for a test). That is 1.12 times fewer instructions for a test in a warm process. MAIN: 638, 634, 638 M and 5,675, 5,677, 5,663 M. A second set of 4 runs each of `cold10`: NEW 5,655 to 5,703 M, MAIN 5,663 to 5,689 M. The change is inside the noise.
- **Parse cache.** A temporary print of `parse_cache::counts()` at each new realm (not committed). The fixture, 12 opens, shared or `fresh`: 1 parse, 12 hits. The cache holds across documents in one process. The tree of the 300 KB script is 3.4 MiB.
- `MAX_IDLE` = 2 against 8, measured on a variant fixture where each of 8 pages also loads its own 100 KB chunk (`server_chunks.py` in the scratchpad, not in the repository). 24 opens in the order p1 to p8, three times round. `MAX_IDLE` = 2: 25 parses, 24 hits (every chunk is parsed again at each visit, because 8 other documents ran between two visits). `MAX_IDLE` = 8: 10 parses, 39 hits. Instructions, 5 runs each, median: 3,297 M against 3,052 M (-7%); the runs spread from 2,846 to 4,038 M (see below). Peak RSS (median) 33.1 MiB against 38.5 MiB (+5.4 MiB, the cache holds 13.2 MB of trees against 7.2 MB). I did not change it: the gain is inside the spread, it exists only for a suite that visits more than 3 different chunk sets in turn, and it costs memory. A cache that evicts by age in bytes under the 32 MiB cap (not by realms) would give both; that is a parser-side change and not in this task.
- The reply to the task's check "two pages of one site": see the `bare-mcp` test. Second open: 0 requests for the `public` script; `fresh`: 1.

### Checks

- `cargo test --release -p bare-net -p bare-mcp -p bare-drive`: all pass. `crates/drive/tests/cache.rs` failed after my first version of the change (a private stale script with an `ETag` was fetched in full by a second open). The fix is the rule above (the stored reply may still be asked about); the test passes and it is unchanged. `survive_limit` `a_page_that_aborts_task_after_task_fails_the_step_with_the_reason` failed once under load (65 s for a test that plans for 45 s) and passed alone in 70 s.
- After the rebase on `e6b3f707`: `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 3,778 passed and 7 failed. The 7 are the OpenSSL TLS tests that fail on main (`bare-net` `https_openssl` 2, `bare-tls` `client_openssl` 4, `tls12_openssl` 1). I ran `https_openssl` and `client_openssl` on `8eb90c9c` and the same 2 and 4 tests fail there; I did not rerun `tls12_openssl` on main.
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` against `e6b3f707` (the main this branch sits on): 803 rows, mean change glibc -0.003%, jemalloc +0.000%, no row over the limit. The 2 rows `examples/parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` do not run on either tree.
- Cookie isolation: `crates/drive/tests/fixture_journey.rs` and the `bare-mcp` login tests pass with the shared client. The fixture shows `login_posts` right.

### Not tested

- An https site (TLS handshake and root load for each `open` before the change): the fixture is plain HTTP.
- A late reply of a request of an old document: the page is dropped before the new one starts, and I wrote no test for a reply in flight.
- Window mode: the parse cache is in the thread of the window. `start` closes the old window and opens a new thread, so by the code the cache is lost between MCP opens in a window (hypothesis, not measured). The headless MCP and the step runner keep it.
- A real site whose scripts have `Cache-Control: max-age=N` and no `public`: they are not shared between two opens that have different jars (see the decision).

### Noticed, not changed

- The instruction count of a `bare-mcp` run depends on wall time: with the same input I saw 2,846 to 4,038 M in 24 opens under load, and 981 +/- 2 M in 10 opens on a quieter machine. The idle slice of the live page (decision of 2026-11-13, "A live page goes on between tool calls") runs while the server waits for the next request. Compare MCP runs on instructions only with a few runs and the minimum.
- A client that is new for each open grows memory by 0.3 MiB for each open (above).
- The reply cache still empties itself when one reply does not fit (design-suite.md, section 2.4).

## 2026-11-13: downloads, steps 1 and 2 (resume, retry, parallel ranges)

Built in one PR, because the two steps share the segment code. Design: `docs/design-downloads.md`.

What changed:
- `downloads/run.rs`: a download from the network runs on threads of its own, not on a page worker. A coordinator thread splits the largest running range when a connection is free (work stealing). Each range thread resumes from its last byte with `Range` and `If-Range`, after 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 s, or `Retry-After`. A `200` to a range request restarts the job from 0, once. A `403` gives the range back to the connection before it. A job without ranges restarts from 0, once. Writes go to `NAME.part` at their offset; the file is renamed at the end.
- `bare-net`: `Client::allow_big` lets a reply declare more than 128 MiB. `Body::unlimited` lifts the 128 MiB and 120 s caps of one body. `Client::fork_alone` gives a client with its own connections, so each range has its own TCP connection, also on HTTP/2 servers.
- Found while building: before this change every download over 128 MiB failed at once, and a slow one failed after 120 s. The 1 GiB `MAX_DOWNLOAD` could never be reached.
- `bare-mcp` `downloads`: a running download shows its bytes and its size.

Benchmark (archMachine, load average 24 to 31, `bare-mcp` click on a link, 3 runs each). BASE `b6ec7df9` (main), NEW this branch. Fixture: `/data/bare-tmp/design/downloads/server.py`, 64 MiB, 4 MiB/s for each connection.

| Case | BASE | NEW |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No cut | 16.01, 16.01, 16.01 s | 2.02, 2.03, 2.04 s |
| Requests 1 and 3 cut after 1 MiB | failed (3 of 3) | 3.06, 3.07, 3.06 s (one 1 s retry wait) |
| Peak RSS of `bare-mcp` | 15 to 16 MiB | 16 MiB |

All NEW files have the expected MD5. Wall time is the link time of the fixture, not CPU, so the load does not change it.
Real server, 1 run: kernel.org `linux-6.12.tar.xz` (147,906,904 bytes, HTTP/2). BASE failed in 0.24 s (the 128 MiB cap). NEW finished in 16.17 s, and its SHA-256 matches `sha256sums.asc`. proof.ovh.net did not answer from this machine during the run (`curl` timed out too).

Checks: `cargo test --release -p bare --lib downloads` (17 pass, 3 runs). `bare-net`, `bare-drive`, `bare-mcp` tests pass except `https_openssl` 2 (the known openssl failures of this machine). `survive_limit::a_page_that_aborts_task_after_task_fails_the_step_with_the_reason` failed once under load average 31 and passed alone.
New tests: one request for a small file, resume after a cut, a split over 4 or more connections, a changed file, a restart without ranges, a refused range, a failed download leaves no file, a reply over 128 MiB.

Not tested: instruction counts of the login journeys (every navigation of a session with downloads now makes one client fork; no journey was measured). A Windows build (`seek_write`). A server that sends a weak ETag only, or `Last-Modified` only. Many downloads at once against the 16-connection limit. The tests were written with the code, not before it.

## 2026-11-13: downloads, step 3 (queue and controls)

Design: `docs/design-downloads.md`, section 5.5.

What changed:
- `DownloadState` has `Queued`, `Paused` and `Cancelled`. At most 3 jobs of one `Downloads` run at once (`MAX_JOBS`); more wait in order. A queued job keeps its first reply unread; when its turn comes, a dead connection resumes like any cut.
- `Downloads::pause`, `resume`, `cancel` and `limit`. Pause starts a new generation, so the range threads stop after their next piece; the bytes and the segment list stay. Resume starts the ranges again from their last byte. A job that cannot resume (no ranges, no validator, a coding or a POST) cannot pause. Cancel removes the file; a queued job leaves the queue. The limit is a token bucket for the whole job (all its connections).
- `bare-mcp` `downloads`: each line has a `#number`. `op` = `list`, `pause`, `resume`, `cancel` or `limit` (`bytes_per_second`), with `id` = the number. `running()` counts queued downloads, so `act` waits for them; a paused one does not hold `act`.
- A paused job keeps its place in the 3. Hypothesis: this is rare enough; change it if a journey needs more.

Checks: `cargo test --release -p bare --lib downloads` (22 pass, 3 runs). New tests: a fourth download waits and all 4 end correct; a paused download keeps its bytes (no change for 400 ms) and resumes with ranges that do not start at 0; a cancelled download leaves no file; a 2 MiB/s limit makes a 0.25 s download take more than 1.2 s; a download without ranges refuses pause. `bare-mcp` and `bare-drive` tests pass; the `bare-mcp` download test also checks the `#1` numbers and the errors of `op`.

By hand through `bare-mcp` (`/data/bare-tmp/design/downloads/controls.py`, 64 MiB at 1 MiB/s for each connection, 1 run): pause held the bytes at 8,807,904 for 1 s; after resume with a 1 MiB/s limit the count grew by 2,334,496 bytes in 2 s; with the limit off the file ended with the expected MD5.

Not tested: a speed limit over many connections against a real server; a queued job whose first connection died while it waited (covered only by the resume path). Not benchmarked: the queue and the controls do not change the transfer path, except one lock-held subtraction for each piece when a limit is set.

## Suite benchmark: shared login, warm workers (step 7, 2026-11-13)

Branch `t3/suite-benchmark-workers`. Design: `docs/design-suite.md`, sections 4, 5 and 9 (owner decisions). Decision: `docs/decisions.md`, "A suite runs in warm worker processes with one shared login".

### What was built

- `tools/suite/server.py`: the fixture app. Login form, `sid` cookie, 8 pages, a notes page that posts through `fetch`, `/logout` that ends the server session, the two public immutable assets (300 KB script, 60 KB sheet), `--login-ms`, `--js-kb`, `--css-kb`, and `/__stats` (login POSTs, requests). Head and body go out in one send (a two-send server adds 41 ms to each reply).
- `tools/suite/gen_suite.py` and `tools/suite/tests/`: 40 tests and `setup.steps`. 26 read, 2 iso (the first leaves a cookie and storage behind, the second must not see them), 4 text, 4 write, 2 sign-out, 1 wrong password, 1 marked `# own` by hand. A shared test starts with `open ${BASE}/home state="${STATE}"`.
- `crates/drive/src/suite.rs` and the flags of `bare-drive`: `--suite DIR [--workers K|auto] [--test-timeout MS] [--login-each] [--only TEXT] [--perf] [--list] [--cold OUTDIR]`.
  - The setup runs once, in worker 0, and saves the session to `OUT/state.json`. The file is deleted at the end.
  - The lint (`lint`) marks a test `own` when a step (not a comment) says `sign out`, `password` or `delete`. A line `# own` or `# shared` in the file decides. For an own test the runner replaces the first `open ... state=` line with the steps of the setup, so the test logs in itself. A test with no `state=` line runs as it is.
  - A worker is a `bare-drive --suite-worker` process. It reads a test name for each line on stdin, runs the test in a new `Session` with a fork of the one network client of the process, and writes one JSON line. The parse caches are thread-local, so they stay warm across its tests.
  - Isolation (design A): each `open` has its own storage and cookie jar. A test that fails, or runs past `--test-timeout`, ends its worker; the next test gets a new process.
  - Queue: each worker thread of the coordinator takes the next test (no fixed split).
  - K by `pick_workers`: `min(cores - 4, half of MemAvailable / peak RSS of worker 0 after the setup, tests)`. The 4 cores are for a local fixture server, the coordinator and the other users of the machine. On this machine: min(12, 324, 40) = 12.
  - Summary (JSON on stdout and `OUT/suite.json`; a table on stderr): each test (class, why, ms, worker, failure), wall time, expected login POSTs, and for each worker its tests, peak RSS and (with `--perf`) instructions. `--perf` puts `perf stat -e instructions:u` around each worker. The sum matched an outer `perf stat` (15,860 M against 15,864 M at K = 4).
- `tools/suite/run.py`: the benchmark. It starts the fixture, runs V0 to V4, and checks the login POSTs and the passed tests of each run (a run that fails a check does not count).
- Tests (`crates/drive/tests/suite.rs`, 5; `suite.rs` unit tests, 3): shared tests start from one login and an own test logs in itself (2 login POSTs in all); a test sees no cookie or storage of the test before it, in the same worker; a failed test ends its worker and the next test runs in worker 1; a sign-out test that `# shared` forces onto the shared session makes the next test fail (no false pass); K workers share the queue.

### Numbers (criterion 7)

Machine archMachine, 16 cores, shared: load average 14 to 22 during the runs, so wall times are weak. Instruction counts are stable (0.1% between runs). Binary: this branch on `ad8c9a4b`, release. 40 tests, 3 runs, median and (min-max). Every run passed 40 of 40, and the server counted the expected login POSTs: 40 for V0, V1 and V3, 5 (the setup and 4 own tests) for V2 and V4.

| Variant | What | Wall s | Instructions (M) | Peak RSS of a worker (MiB) | Against V0: wall, instructions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| V0 | a new process for each test, every test logs in, one at a time | 4.30 (4.13-6.11) | 21,175 (21,175-21,176) | 26.0 | 1.00, 1.00 |
| V1 | one warm worker, every test logs in | 3.48 (3.12-5.27) | 18,277 (18,244-18,282) | 26.5 | 1.23, 1.16 |
| V2 | one warm worker, one shared login | 3.13 (3.07-4.41) | 15,682 (15,660-15,689) | 26.4 | 1.37, **1.35** |
| V3 K = 2 / 4 / 8 / 12 | V0 with K processes at a time | 3.07 / 3.83 / 2.33 / 1.64 | 21,155 / 21,164 / 21,155 / 21,178 | 26.0 | 1.40 / 1.12 / 1.84 / 2.63, 1.00 |
| V4 K = 2 | warm workers, shared login | 2.62 (1.71-2.92) | 15,756 | 26.6 | 1.64, 1.34 |
| V4 K = 4 | the same | 0.91 (0.83-0.94) | 15,933 | 26.4 | **4.73**, 1.33 |
| V4 K = 8 | the same | 0.63 (0.60-0.63) | 16,233 | 26.5 | **6.85**, 1.30 |
| V4 K = 12 (the default K here) | the same | 0.57 (0.57-0.64) | 16,451 (16,261-16,532) | 26.3 (317 MiB for 12 workers) | **7.51**, 1.29 |

The frozen baseline `f6415364` gives the same V0: 21,160 M (21,135-21,161), 4.17 s (4.11-6.68), 25.7 MiB. A run of the default (`--workers auto`) took 445 ms for 40 tests with 12 workers.

**Verdict, wall time: met** for K = 4 or more (4.7 to 7.5 times against V0, median of 3, load 14 to 22). Not met at K = 2 (1.64 times), and not met with one worker on this fixture (1.37 times). The wall result is a result of the pool, not of the engine (design-suite.md, section 8, question 1).
**Verdict, instructions with one worker: not met on the standard suite.** V2 is 1.35 times lower than V0 (target 1.5). Workers add instructions, not remove them: 12 workers parse the 300 KB script 12 times (+5% at K = 12).

Why 1.35: a document costs about 75 M here (design-suite.md, section 1.2). A V0 test is 7 documents (login page, home and 5 pages) and a V2 test is 6, plus the first parse of the script (71 M) that V0 pays in each process and V2 pays once. The 4 own tests pay their login. That is the 1.35 (V1, warm only, gives 1.16; the shared login gives the other 1.16).

Sensitivity (same fixture, other suites; 3 runs each; instruction ratio against V0 of that suite). These are not the verdict; they show what moves it.

| Suite | V0 (M) | V2 (M) | V2 ratio | V4 K = 4 | V4 K = 8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| standard (5 pages after the start) | 21,175 | 15,682 | 1.35 | 1.33 | 1.30 |
| the 26 `read` tests only (ceiling of 100% shared) | 16,608 | 12,914 | 1.29 | 1.26 | 1.24 |
| 2 pages after the start | 14,699 | 9,226 | 1.59 | 1.55 | 1.50 |
| 1 page after the start | 12,569 | 7,091 | 1.77 | 1.72 | 1.65 |
| standard, `--login-ms 300` (wall: V0 20.0 s, V2 6.74 s, V4 K = 4 1.50 s) | 21,169 | 15,602 | 1.36 | 1.33 | 1.31 |

The ratio grows when the test is shorter or the login is a larger part of it. The `read` tests alone give less than the whole suite because a `read` test is the longest class (5 pages). A slow server login makes setup reuse alone cut wall time 3 times (V2 against V0) and the pool 13 times at K = 4. K = 8 was slower than K = 4 there (1.79 s against 1.50 s, load 17 to 18): hypothesis, the single-process Python fixture and the other jobs of the machine; not checked.

### Checks

- After the rebase on `c8a75edd`: `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 3,797 passed, 10 failed, none in `bare-drive` (its 5 new integration tests and 3 new unit tests pass). 7 of the 10 are the OpenSSL TLS tests (`bare-net` `https_openssl` 2, `bare-tls` `client_openssl` 4, `tls12_openssl` 1) that the notes of the shared-client change show failing on main; I did not run them on main again. The other 3 failed under load (14 to 22) and pass alone: `bare` `downloads::run::tests::a_changed_file_starts_again_from_zero`, `bare-mcp` `a_snapshot_of_5000_elements_takes_under_30_ms`, `bare-net` `h2_node_edge` `a_server_that_closes_idle_sessions_does_not_break_the_next_request`.
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh`, `test262_check.sh` and `exec_diff.sh` were not run: the change touches only `crates/drive` (the `bare-drive` binary and its tests) and `tools/suite`, and no engine crate or `bare-stress` links it.
- `tools/portable_check.sh --scan`: ok (the suite code has no OS code; `/proc/meminfo` and `VmHWM` are read in `main.rs`, which is on the list).
- A sign-out test that a user forces onto the shared login makes the next shared test fail on its first check (`expect ... Heading home` meets the login page). That is the "no false pass" gate. The runner does not log in again: see below.

### Not tested, not built

- A real login or a real network. The fixture login is cheap (p = 0.12 by design-suite.md); the 300 ms row only adds server wait.
- Wall time on an idle machine. The load was 14 to 22.
- Re-login after a stale shared session (design-suite.md, section 4.3: "if the check fails, log in again once"): not built. A stale session fails the tests that start from it, and the summary says so.
- Slowest-first order from the times of the last run: not built (the given order is used).
- A worker restart after M tests for memory growth: not built. Peak RSS per worker is in the summary.
- A hung test with `--perf`: the coordinator kills the `perf` process and not its child. Without `--perf` the worker is killed (tested only by the failed-test case, not by a timeout).
- `--window`, Windows and macOS runs. The suite code builds on every target (no OS code in it), but only Linux ran.
- The MCP tool `run_suite` (owner decision 3): next, as a separate PR.
- Per-worker accounts (design B) and the `write` class with one account for each worker: the write tests add a note with a unique text and check that text, so they do not depend on the other writers.

### Noticed, not changed

- The reply cache still empties itself when one reply does not fit.
- The steps of a composed own test have other line numbers than the test file (the setup is inserted before them); a failure names the line of the composed text.

## 2026-11-13: cheap CSSOM objects (shared declaration prototype, rule objects on demand)

Step 3 of `docs/perf-goal.md` (second part), `design-style.md` section 3.5 and phase 5.

### What was built

- A rule declaration (`rule.style`) has no own accessors. It uses the one `CSSStyleDeclaration` prototype of `el.style`. The internal slot is the rule id (`browser_style.rs` hooks `declaration_written` after each write).
- `cssRules` and `cssRules.length` make no rule object. `cssRules[i]` makes one and caches it. The list keeps a 12-byte `Entry::Chunk(start, end)` span for each rule that JS has not read. The length stays exact: a validity parse of the chunk skips a rule that does not parse. An unread rule is published verbatim from its chunk text.
- A declaration is made on the first read of `rule.style`. It costs one detached DOM node and is not counted by the wrapper limit.
- `MAX_OBJECTS` goes from 65,536 to 1 << 19. `MAX_RULES` is 1 << 21 (24 MiB of entries). Why: a rule that is read costs 585 B (selector only) to about 0.9 KB (with `.style`). 187,852 rules cost 585 B each, so the worst case at the cap is about 290 MiB. The `style-objects` limit (65,536) stays and binds first when a page reads `.style` of more than about 65,000 rules.
- Decision: `decisions.md`. `design-style.md` is corrected: Chrome has the CSS properties as own enumerable keys on each declaration. The shared prototype matches bare `el.style` and not Chrome. This is a known difference. No journey depends on it (checked: 2 of 48 journeys use the CSSOM at all, by a trace build).

### Numbers

`sheety_16383` (16 MiB sheet) with the `cssRules` read, 3 runs each, machine archMachine. Peak RSS by `wait4`, instructions by `perf stat -e instructions:u`.

| Build | Peak RSS (range) | Instructions | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BASE `f6415364` | 970 MiB (969,904 to 970,576 KiB) | 18.18 G | stops on `cssom-objects` |
| MAIN `1ea36fda` | 973 MiB (972,972 to 973,416 KiB) | 20.52 G | stops on `cssom-objects` |
| NEW | 272 MiB (278,468 to 279,004 KiB) | 10.10 G | passes |

Criterion 5 (300 MiB or lower): met, 272 MiB. `sheety_8192`: BASE 848 MB and 14.37 G, MAIN 851 MB and 16.71 G, NEW 147 MB and 5.08 G. Cost per rule before: 10.2 KB. After: 585 B (selector read), about 0.9 KB (with `.style`).

Criterion 8 (cap by the rule count): the cap is now set by cost, with one limit (`style-objects`) that still binds at about 65,000 declarations.

Journeys, live (the step-1 corpus runner is not on main), 3 runs each, min of 3, MAIN `a7ba0525` and NEW: 46 of 48 pass on both. `hn-front` and `hn-new-past` fail in all 3 runs on both builds (cause not examined). Total 23,878 M and 24,303 M (+1.8%). The sum is live noise: the same journey moves more between runs than between builds. `paulgraham-home` is 44 M and 61 M on NEW, but the same binary of MAIN `1ea36fda` also gives 43.9 M and 61.0 M in two runs. `go-dev-home` varies 121 to 271 M on MAIN. This total is not a clean A/B and must not be read as one. 2 of 48 journeys touch the CSSOM, so the journeys are not the place where this change shows.

Cost matrix `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` against `1ea36fda`: 803 rows, mean change +0.004%. Rows over 0.5%: `dataset_load keys 1000 50` +0.60% and `keys 10000 50` +0.63%, `resources_load small 1` +1.7% and `small 10` +2.2%. I think all four are codegen or timing noise, not CSSOM cost:
- The two `dataset_load` rows do not call CSSOM code. I tried `#[inline(never)]` on the CSSOM `len`, `item` and `fill`: no change. Base commits swing -0.6% to +2.9% on this row.
- `resources_load small 1` run 3 times on each build outside the matrix: 6.87 to 6.89 M on both.
Two rows (`parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`) do not run. I did not diagnose them.

## Sheet registry (2026-11-13)

Step 2 of `docs/perf-goal.md`, phase 1 of `docs/design-style.md`. Branch `t3/document-sheet-registry`.

### What was built

- The document keeps the list of its `<link>`, `<style>` and `<base>` elements that are in the tree, in the order of the page: `Document::sheet_nodes()` (`crates/html/src/dom.rs`). A shadow tree comes right after its host.
- Each entry says whether the element is in the light tree (`light`) and whether a loader scan may use it (`html`: light tree, HTML namespace, no `template` above it).
- Three code paths read it and do not walk the DOM any more: `Run::tell_links` (`browser_loader/sheets.rs`), `cascade::sources_capped` (called by `plan`) and `resources::document_base`. Attributes and the text of the elements are read when needed, so the list holds only structure.
- How it stays exact. The name of an element never changes. So the list of all elements with these three names is exact. It is found by one pass over the new part of the node `Vec` at a read (`scan_sheets`), so a document that nobody asks pays nothing. Which of them are in the tree, and in which order, is made at a read and dropped when a change can alter it: `link` and `detach` of a node that has children or has one of the three names (only after a first read), `parse_cut`/`parse_open`/`parse_close`, `attach_shadow` and `set_foreign`. There is no second mutation system: these are the places where the tree changes.
- Two ways to make the list. A page with few nodes for each element (nodes < 32 x elements) takes a walk. A big page climbs from each element to the top node and visits only the ancestors (cost: depth of each element plus the children of those ancestors, up to the last one that leads to an element). The cost of the walk on a small page is lower than the tables of the other way (the first version used the tables always: `preload_load style 10` +41% instructions).
- No `href` index. The design (L3) asked for `HashMap<href, nodes>`. The list has only the L elements of one page (under 30 usually), `tell_links` filters it by `href` in O(L), and an index needs a drop on every `href` change. At S = 200 sheets and L = 200 links that is 40 k string compares in all. Decision: no index. Recorded in `docs/decisions.md`.
- The correctness guard: in a debug build and in `bare-html` tests, each read of `sheet_nodes()` compares the list with `sheet_nodes_walk()` (a walk of the whole tree), for both ways of making it. A change that is missed fails the test.

### Numbers

Machine archMachine, shared with other build agents (instruction counts are not affected, wall time is). BASE `f6415364`, MAIN `e6b3f707` (the main this branch sits on), NEW this branch.

**Sheet ramp** (new, `/data/bare-tmp/sheet-reg/www/r_<nodes>_<sheets>.html`): a script builds N `div`s, then adds S `<link rel=stylesheet>` to the head; the page is done when S `load` events came. Local server, `bare-drive`, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, 3 runs, minimum (spread = max/min).

| nodes | sheets | MAIN (M instr) | NEW (M instr) | MAIN / NEW | peak RSS MAIN / NEW (MiB) |

| 5,000 | 200 | 525 (1.08) | 156 (1.05) | 3.4x | 15.8 / 15.3 |
| 10,000 | 200 | 948 (1.04) | 220 (1.11) | 4.3x | 16.8 / 17.0 |
| 20,000 | 50 | 628 (1.12) | 254 (1.01) | 2.5x | 18.5 / 18.3 |

A first run before the rebase gave 26.06 / 25.49 / 24.49 G for the same set.

**Where the gain is.** A profile (`perf record`, 200 k instruction period) of `rust-book-search`: `tell_links` is 9.4% of the instructions on MAIN and absent on NEW. A profile of `python-org-docs-link` today: `tell_links` 0.8% on MAIN (the profile of 2026-11-13 had 30.5% loader share; the site changed, or that share was not `tell_links`: hypothesis). So **success criterion 4 (1.3x on the heavy-scan journeys) is not shown on the live pages of today**. The sheet ramp shows 2.5x to 5.7x where the scans are heavy. The journeys total gains 3.0% against MAIN. The estimate of the design (8 to 9 points) is above this result: the node visits of the walks were 23.9 M over 43 journeys, but in instructions they are about 3% of the total, not 8%.

**Cost matrix** (`tools/js/cost_matrix.sh`, MAIN `e6b3f707` vs NEW, 803 rows): mean change glibc -0.010%, jemalloc +0.000%, 0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators. 2 rows do not run on either tree (`examples/parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`: stack overflow, exit 134 on MAIN too). The first full run found a regression: +0.9% to +1.4% on `fragment_load parse`, `browser_load svgparse` and `resources_load dups`, and +41% on `preload_load style 10`. The cause was a check at each node creation and the tables of the big-page way on a small page. Both are gone (lazy scan; the walk for small pages).

## The `run_suite` tool of bare-mcp (owner decision 3 of `docs/design-suite.md`, section 9)

### What was built

`bare-mcp` has a tool `run_suite`: `dir` (required), `workers` (a number or `"auto"`), `filter` (a part of a test name), `perf` (bool), and `vars`, `secrets_file`, `width`, `height`, `timeout_ms`, `test_timeout_ms`. It runs the suite through `bare_drive::suite::run_report`, the same code as `bare-drive --suite`. The reply is a short text: `ok|FAILED P/N passed, K workers, MS ms, logins L`, one line for each failure (test, step line, kind, message; at most 20 and 300 characters each), and the peak RSS of each worker. It is cut at 3000 characters. For a failure it also gives the capture folder (`out:`); a passed run leaves no folder.

Library change in `crates/drive/src/suite.rs` (small, no change of runner behavior): `run` split into `run_report(&Config) -> Result<Value, String>` (prints nothing) and `run` (prints the JSON, gives the exit code). `Config` has a new field `exe: Option<PathBuf>`: the program that runs as a worker.

### Choice: the coordinator is a library call; the workers are a shell-out

The workers must be `bare-drive --suite-worker` processes, and `spawn` started `current_exe()`. In `bare-mcp` that is `bare-mcp`, which has no worker role. The code forces a process here (a worker is one process that is killed on a timeout or a failure). So the MCP server starts `bare-drive` from `BARE_DRIVE`, else the file next to `bare-mcp`. If it is missing, the tool says so and names the build command. The other option was a worker role in `bare-mcp` that repeats the option parsing of `bare-drive`; I did not take it.

### Choice: the call blocks the server loop; the live sessions are not touched

The run is one reply to one request, as `run_steps` is. The server loop does not tick the live pages meanwhile (their timers run late, then catch up). The suite uses its own processes, network client, temp folder and `STATE` file. It does not read or write `live` or `saved`. A test checks that `sessions` and a live `read` are the same after three runs. A non-blocking run (a thread and a later reply) needs MCP progress or a polling tool; not built.

### Checks

- New test `run_suite_gives_a_short_summary_and_names_a_failing_step_and_leaves_live_sessions_alone` (`crates/mcp/tests/server.rs`): the `tools/suite` fixture server, `setup.steps` and two read tests of `tools/suite/tests`, and one broken test. It checks `FAILED 2/3 passed, 2 workers`, `logins 1`, the failing test with step line 3, no secret, the `filter`, the error for a filter that matches nothing, and the unchanged live session.
- `cargo test --release -p bare-mcp -p bare-drive` (`server`, `suite`, lib): all pass.

### Not tested

`perf: true` (needs `perf`), `workers: "auto"`, a suite with an own test through MCP, a test that times out through MCP, Windows and macOS paths for the `bare-drive` lookup, `cargo test --release --workspace`, the cost matrix (no engine change, no change in the browser path).
## Repeatable journey benchmark: record, replay, compare (2026-11-13)

Branch `t3/repeatable-journey-benchmarks`. Step 1 of `docs/perf-goal.md` (the benchmark contract), minus the login fixture, the render-trigger counters and the per-origin cost.

### What was built

- Record and replay at the HTTP layer (`crates/net/src/replay.rs`, hook in `Client::start`). `BARE_NET_RECORD=<dir>` stores each reply. `BARE_NET_REPLAY=<dir>` serves them with no network. `BARE_NET_FILL=<dir>` serves what is stored and fetches only a miss, then stores it. Fill is the precedence winner, then replay, then record.
- A request has a label: method, URL and a hash of its body. The same label is served in recorded order, then the last reply repeats. A miss is an error on the page and a line on stderr: `bare-net: replay: no recorded reply for <label>`.
- The stored body is the raw body: after dechunking, before `Content-Encoding`. A replay decodes it again, so the decode cost stays in the measurement. Redirects, `Set-Cookie`, a cut body (with its `io::ErrorKind`) and a failed request replay as they were. This browser has no WebSocket. `EventSource` is a shim over `fetch`, so it goes through the tape. A long-poll or a stream that is still open when the page goes away is stored as a cut body (`TimedOut`) and replays as one.
- Determinism in replay mode: `BARE_SEED=<n>` fixes `Math.random`, `crypto.getRandomValues`, `crypto.randomUUID` and multipart boundaries (TLS random is unchanged). With a tape set, `bare-drive` settles pending pictures between steps and at the end, and waits for the requests in flight at the end (`Client::drain`). Background image jobs raced the exit and the next step before this.
- Runner `tools/bench/journeys.sh` (`journeys.py`): `record`, `fill`, `run` and `compare`. Each run is a new process (cold). The TSV holds journey, run, pass, instructions (`perf stat -e instructions:u`), cpu ms, wall ms, peak RSS (`wait4`), PSS and the miss count. PSS is sampled in its own run (run 0) because reading `smaps_rollup` changes thread timing and the instruction count.
- Corpus: `/data/bare-tmp/corpus/main`, 47 journeys recorded with `bare-drive` of main at `cc8cd9d0`. It is machine-local and not in the repository.
- Baseline: `f6415364` plus the replay patch, as local branch `bench-base-replay` (worktree `/data/bare-tmp/bench-base-src`, target `/data/bare-tmp/target-bench-base`, binary `/data/bare-tmp/bare-drive-journeys-base`). It is not pushed. The patch is the net, drive and seed changes of this PR, cherry-picked.
- `wikipedia-main-random.steps`: the last `expect` also needs `!location.pathname.endsWith('Main_Page')`. The old check passed with no random page.

### How to use it

    tools/bench/journeys.sh record  <bare-drive>                 # live sites, then fill rounds
    tools/bench/journeys.sh run     --runs 3 --pss <bare-drive>
    tools/bench/journeys.sh compare --runs 3 --pss --out cmp.tsv <base bare-drive> <new bare-drive>

### Result: 3 runs each, baseline vs main

Machine: archMachine, loopback replay, `heavy` lock held. 47 journeys, cold runs, runs interleaved. Medians. Log: `/data/bare-tmp/corpus/compare-final.{log,tsv}`.

| | baseline `f6415364` + replay | main `cc8cd9d0` | change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Instructions, sum of medians | 74,004 M | 71,981 M | -2.7% |
| CPU (user+system), sum of medians | 16,642 ms | 16,418 ms | -1.3% |
| Wall, sum of medians | 21,096 ms | 22,463 ms | +6.5% (loaded machine: a test build ran at the start) |
| PSS, sum of medians | 1,675 MiB | 1,719 MiB | +2.6% |
| Peak RSS, sum of medians | 1,824 MiB | 1,895 MiB | +3.9% |

The totals are not a verdict on main: the same-binary spread below is larger than the change.

### Same-binary variation (target: under 2% instructions per journey)

Target not met. Spread is (max - min) / median over 3 runs of one binary. The worst side of each journey counts.

- Under 2%: 19 of 47. Over 2%: 28. Over 5%: 20.
- Over 5% (base / new): `archlinux-org-home` 31/1, `craigslist-home` 0/16, `crates-io-home` 14/71, `devto-home` 2/7, `github-docs-home` 6/1, `hn-comments-back` 6/6, `hn-front` 3/8, `kernel-org-home` 0/6, `mdn-reference` 16/70, `nodejs-org-home` 40/20, `python-docs-search` 1/99, `react-docs` 22/6, `rust-book-chapters` 1/17, `rust-book-search` 245/331, `substack-home` 7/7, `wikipedia-main-random` 10/3, `wikipedia-portal` 13/7, `wikipedia-search` 9/6, `wikipedia-toc-languages` 8/10, `wiktionary-portal` 18/18.
- The runs fall into a few distinct values, not a smooth spread. Example, `python-docs-search`: 188 M, 183 M, 184 M on the baseline and 2,160 M, 2,154 M, 1,986 M, 188 M on main. A page reaches or misses work (a debounced search, a script that runs a search index) depending on when its timer fires against the other threads.
- Cause (hypothesis, from the discrete modes, the zero-miss runs and the profiles of the earlier runs): page timers and debounces run on the real clock, so the order of timers, worker threads and the end of the journey changes between runs. Images (fixed here) and random ids (fixed here) were the two earlier causes. `rust-book-search` is the clearest case: 3.9 G to 19.7 G with identical inputs.
- A second cause, for `crates-io-home` and `mdn-reference` (and in part `wikipedia-*`): the set of requests varies, so a replay has misses. Analytics beacons with a time or an id in the body never match (`wikipedia-*`, `go-dev-home`, `mdn-reference`). They are constant, harmless errors. A page that asks for a file that no recording run reached shows up as a miss in only some runs (`crates-io-home`, `mdn-reference`).
- Not fixed, because it needs a design decision: a virtual clock for page timers in replay mode (jump to the next timer when the page is idle). I judged it out of scope for this task. It would remove the timer races, and it would change what "time to ready" means.

### Journeys that pass live and cannot pass on replay

- `nextjs-docs`: the engine stops the page at `checkVisibility`. Live latency hides it, and a fast replay reaches it. It is not in the corpus. This is an engine issue, not a replay issue.

### Checks

- `cargo test --release -p bare-net`: the unit tests of the tape and `crates/net/tests/replay.rs` (record then replay a loopback server with a redirect, gzip, a cookie and a POST; a miss is the clear error; a cut body and a failed request replay as they were; fill fetches only the miss).
- `crates/drive/tests/replay.rs`: a journey records against a loopback server, replays with no connection to it, and a page that was not recorded fails with the miss error.

- Rebase: only `docs/progress.md` conflicted. `crates/net/src/http.rs` merged with no conflict. The jar-keyed reply cache of #483 is above the tape hook, so both work: a reply from the cache never reaches the tape, and a miss goes to the tape first and then to the network.
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: all pass except 3 groups that also fail on main `c8a75edd`/`3c958f96` on this machine: `bare-net --test https_openssl` (2 tests), `bare-tls --test client_openssl` (4), `bare-tls --test tls12_openssl` (1).
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` (main `3c958f96` vs this branch): 803 rows, mean change glibc -0.002%, 0 rows over the limit under either allocator. 2 rows (`parse_load deep 1`, `deep 10`) fail to run on both trees with a stack overflow.
- `TEST262=/data/claude-tmp/test262 tools/js/test262_check.sh`: gate ok (the checkout is at the commit the subset names). `tools/js/exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences.

## Who forces style and layout (step 6.0, 2026-11-14)

Branch `t3/count-style-layout`. Design: `docs/design-suite.md`, section 3.5 and decision 7. This is the count that decides whether the styles-only frame is built. No behavior changes.

### What was built

- `crates/bare/src/force.rs`: counters for each style pass and each layout pass, off unless `BARE_FORCE_STATS` is set. With it set, each pass writes one line to stderr with its caller, the elements styled or boxes laid out, and the user instructions of the pass (`perf_event_open`, Linux x86-64; 0 elsewhere). Hook points: `cascade_inner` (outcomes `hit`, `restyle`, `compute`, `plan`, `rules`), `layout_at` (`full`, `kept`) and `layout_shared` (`hit`).
- A caller is the `file:line` of a window frame request (`#[track_caller]` on `Page::frame_now`, `inspect`, `visible_box`, `hit`, `rehover` and `scroll_with`), or the name of a script API (`getComputedStyle`, `offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect`, the motion step, the observers). The outermost caller wins.
- `tools/drive/force_count.py BARE_DRIVE [--corpus DIR | --suite DIR]`: runs the journeys (live, or replayed from the corpus of `tools/bench/journeys.sh`) or the suite with one worker, each process under `perf stat -e instructions:u`, and adds the passes up by caller. It also finds the layouts that a styles-only frame would not make: a frame layout that was built for an `inspect` request (locators, snapshot, find, read) and that no geometry step used before the next layout.
- Cost with the switch off: the suite V2 (one worker, shared login) is 15,588 to 15,601 M instructions with this change and 15,597 to 15,603 M on main `fe2d54cd` (3 runs each). No difference.

### The count

Machine archMachine, 16 cores, shared. Binary: release, this branch on `fe2d54cd`. Instruction counts per pass hold under load. The journeys on the corpus are not stable between runs (the replay uses real clocks, `docs/decisions.md`, "The journey benchmark replays recorded HTTP replies"): the total of the 47 journeys that pass was 64.1 to 67.7 G in three runs (one earlier run on the same code gave 86 G, with `rust-book-search` at 24.8 G against 16.4 G). `nextjs-docs` fails on the corpus on main too (`status.tsv` says 0), so 47 of 48 are counted. A live run also lost one journey to a network flake (`hn-new-past`, `nextjs-docs`).

| the suite, 40 tests, 1 worker, shared login | 4 | 15,626 to 15,635 M | 34.9% | **30.9%** | 7.1% | **2.69%** (420.6 M, 398 layouts, same in each run) |

### What the count says

1. The driver asks for little of the style and layout. Locators and snapshot (the callers that read only styles) are 2.5% of the corpus journeys. Click, visible, hit test and rehover are 3.4%. The rest comes from the page itself: the motion step (8.9%), script reads of geometry and style (7.2%) and a picture that arrived (6.7%). A styles-only frame cannot touch those.
2. The layout that a styles-only frame would skip is 0.3 to 0.4% of the corpus journeys, about 2.0% of the live journeys and 2.7% of the suite. These are upper bounds. Without the frame, the next geometry step lays out from an older kept layout (`layout_kept`), so it does more work than the one it replaces. The cost of that is not measured. All the skipped layouts of the suite (398 of 398) and 7 of 8 on the corpus come from one request, `locate.rs:222`: the text of an element, read by `expect LOC text`. The poll of that step finds a stale frame about 1,200 times in the live journeys.
3. `Frame.layout` is read at 34 places (`grep 'frame.layout\|f.layout\|fr.layout'`), not the 5 callers that the design counted. An `Option<Layout>` is a change in the paint, hit-test, scroll and screenshot paths too.
4. The rule-set build is the largest cost that the count found, and it is not a layout cost. It is 30.9% of the suite (4.8 G of 15.6 G) and 7.8 to 8.3% of the corpus journeys. A new rule set is built for most documents: 186 builds for the 334 style passes of `locate.rs:222` in the suite. A check with the fixture sheet at 1 KB instead of 60 KB (`tools/suite/server.py --css-kb 1`) gives 322 M for the builds instead of 4,840 M, so the 60 KB sheet costs about 6.5 M instructions for each document (hypothesis: the index of the rules is built again for each document; the parse is cached). The sheet registry (#490) did not change this share. That is the part of criterion 7 that is left for the rule index and the registry (`cascade.rs`, `sources_capped`).
5. Motion frames cost 6.1% of the corpus journeys (52 style passes, 224 K elements styled, 1.8 G in rule-set builds). Hypothesis: a page with no transition or animation does not need them. Not checked.

### Decision

The styles-only frame is not built. Its upper bound is 0.4% on the corpus journeys (the criterion 2 benchmark), 2.0% live and 2.7% on the suite. The rule was: under about 2% does not pay. The suite figure is over 2%, but a real saving is smaller than the bound (point 2), the change is larger than the design said (point 3), and it cannot lift criterion 7 (1.35 to 1.5 times needs 10% of the suite). Property-mask cascade (B) and closure layout (C) stay unbuilt: they need the same style-only share, and it is 2.5% of the corpus journeys. See `docs/decisions.md`.

To check again: `tools/drive/force_count.py` after the rule-set cost falls. The skipped layout is a fixed 420 M on the suite, so its share rises when the other costs fall (about 4% of the suite without the rule-set builds).

### Checks

- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 3,818 passed, 9 failed. Two are downloads tests that fail under load and pass alone, 3 runs each (`a_changed_file_starts_again_from_zero`: "no connection for the download"; `a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved`). Seven are `bare-tls` tests that use `openssl` (`client_openssl`, `tls12_openssl`, `https_openssl`: `BadSignature`; the machine has OpenSSL 4.1.0, hypothesis for the cause). This change touches no file of `crates/tls`, `crates/net`, `crates/mcp` or `downloads/` (`git diff origin/main --stat` is empty for them), so the same code fails on main. Not run on main.
- The counters change no result: the 47 journeys that pass on the corpus pass with the switch, `nextjs-docs` fails on main without it too, and the suite passes 40 of 40 with it (the check of `force_count.py` counts only runs that pass).

### Not tested

- The styles-only frame itself (not built). The extra cost of a larger `layout_kept` after skipped layouts.
- Wall time (not the subject). A second machine. `bare-mcp` sessions (the `snapshot`, `find` and `read` tools): they call the same `inspect`, so the count above covers their frame requests, but no MCP session was run.
- The instruction count of a pass on a CPU without `perf_event_open` for user mode (`perf_event_paranoid` above 2): the counters then print 0 instructions and the counts of passes stay right.
## A virtual page clock for replay mode (2026-11-14)

Branch `t3/deterministic-replay-clock`, on main after #486. Design: `docs/design-virtual-clock.md`. Decision: `docs/decisions.md`. Machine: archMachine, `heavy` lock held, corpus machine-local.

### What was built

- `BARE_CLOCK=virtual` with a tape that reads (`BARE_NET_REPLAY`, `BARE_NET_FILL`): page time (`Date.now`, `performance.now`, timers, frames, loader slice deadlines, driver waits) is a number that only the scheduler, the driver and the reply tasks move. A reply is due 5 ms after it starts. The page sees it only then. A move of the clock waits in real time for the replies due by then.
- `journeys.sh ... --clock real|virtual`. `--clock virtual` uses the corpus `/data/bare-tmp/corpus/virtual` (a copy of `main`, filled with `journeys.sh fill --clock virtual`). The default stays `real` and `corpus/main`.
- Test: `crates/drive/tests/replay.rs` (a page with an 8 s timer ends in under 4 s on replay with the clock on; with the clock off the same step does not end in 3 s). Unit test in `vclock.rs`.

### Cause of the variation

A reply is ready when a worker thread has read the tape and decoded the body. A step of the driver ends by timers and sleeps on the real clock. Which comes first depends on the load. Same binary on the real clock, 6 runs each, instructions in M:

| Journey | Real clock | Virtual clock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rust-book-search` | 3846 3838 3838 3839 3846 3839 (this session); 3.9 G to 19.7 G in the #486 runs | 16532 16531 16531 16532 16532 16531 |
| `python-docs-search` | 175 175 175 1432 175 175 | 2146 2145 2145 2146 2146 2145 |

On the real clock the search index of `rust-book-search` reaches the page after 1 to 6+ of the 9 keys, and the page searches once per key after it. The virtual clock fixes this order. It then shows one mode in all runs (the one where a reply that takes 5 ms arrives after about 5 keys of 1 ms).

### Same-binary spread (3 runs, 47 journeys, new binary)

- Real clock, corpus `main`: 15 of 47 journeys over 2%, 7 over 5% (worst: `wikipedia-search` 34.8%, `wiktionary-portal` 33.0%, `wikipedia-portal` 15.1%, `github-docs-home` 14.5%, `lobsters-front` 8.5%, `nodejs-org-home` 6.7%, `kernel-org-home` 6.4%).
- Virtual clock, corpus `virtual`: 47 of 47 under 2%. The worst is 0.3% (`kernel-org-home`). 40 of 47 was the target. In the baseline-vs-main run below the worst is 0.7% (main) and 3.7% (baseline, `archlinux-org-home`).
- Journeys over 2% on the virtual clock: none. The rest of the variation: run 0 (the PSS run) of `wikipedia-article` and `wikipedia-search` shows 3 and 2 misses that the runs without PSS do not show. PSS reading changes thread timing, and part of the loader is still real time. Run 0 gives no instruction count.
- `wikipedia-portal` has one miss in every run: a POST to `/ins-*/v2/events` whose body hash changes between runs (hypothesis: a value in the body that is not on the virtual clock; cause not found). It does not change the pass result.

### The virtual clock changes the work, not the result

Same binary, real clock on corpus `main` against virtual clock on corpus `virtual`, medians of 3. Total 66,562 M and 96,316 M. The change is not a speed-up or a slow-down. The clock selects the mode of the page, and the real runs ended before some work (journeys that change by more than 10% or that are over 2% on the real clock):

| Journey | Real M | Virtual M |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `nodejs-org-home` | 1,243 | 5,828 |
| `python-docs-search` | 175 | 2,146 |
| `rust-book-search` | 3,846 | 16,531 |
| `react-docs` | 6,004 | 16,727 |
| `github-docs-home` | 2,280 | 5,225 |
| `substack-home` | 842 | 1,468 |
| `mdn-reference` | 8,666 | 6,866 |
| `wikipedia-search` | 8,848 | 6,823 |
| `craigslist-home` | 51 | 20 |

All 47 journeys pass on both clocks. STOP check, finding: with the real-clock recording, `react-docs` fails on the virtual clock (14 recorded replies are missing: chunks that the real run never asked for). It is not a change of result of the page. After `fill --clock virtual` it passes 4 of 4. For that reason the virtual clock has its own corpus. Nothing else changed from pass to fail. `nextjs-docs` is not in either corpus (see the #486 section).

## Step 4: rule bodies are read on first use, and the CSS tokenizer is faster (2026-11-14)

Design: `docs/design-style.md` §3.4 (P2, P4). Branch `t3/lazy-css-declarations`, based on main `fe2d54cd`.

### What changed

- `crates/css/src/scan.rs` (new): a byte-table scanner finds the end of a style rule. It follows the block structure of the tokenizer (strings, comments, `url(`, escapes, nested blocks). It gives up (`Bail`) on anything it is not sure of, and the exact tokenizer reads that rule.
- `parse_stylesheet_lazy`: a style rule keeps its prelude and the text of its block. `RuleSet` parses the selectors at once. It reads the block on the first style that needs it (`RuleSet::ensure`, on a memo miss only). Rules with a block that cannot have a declaration (`a{}`, `a{;;}`, `a{:red}`) make no entry.
- `@media`, `@supports`, `@layer`, `@import` and `@keyframes` are still found at once.
- `has_motion` stays exact: the scanner says whether a block may set `transition-*` or `animation-*`. `has_motion` reads only those blocks, and only when it is asked.
- Tokenizer: ASCII fast paths in `peek`, `name`, `string`, spaces, digits, comments, and a `short_number` path (at most 7 digits, equal to `str::parse::<f32>`).
- `Entry` is 72 bytes (was 80).

### Split of the parse cost (`crates/css/examples/parse_split.rs`, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, reps 11 minus reps 1, over 10)

Declarations are the larger part: about 64% or more of a parse on the six sheets (bootstrap.min, bootstrap, fontawesome, docs-rs-home, debian-org-home, github-docs-home). So P2 and P4 both went ahead.

| `RuleSet::add` | main | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bootstrap.min.css | 42.4 M | 16.6 M |
| github-docs-home sheet | 312.6 M | 103.3 M |
| tokenize, bootstrap.min.css | 17.4 M | 10.4 M |

### Exactness

- Lazy parse equals eager parse: 4 M junk-fuzz rounds plus 3 seeds of 2 M each, and 6.5 MB of real sheets (110 sheets of the journeys), with no difference. The fuzz found 4 bugs before it passed (trailing comment in a prelude, `<!--url(`, NUL before `url(`, a stack-class typo). Each has a test.
- Old tokenizer equals new tokenizer: 3 M fuzz rounds and 10 MB of sheets.
- `has_motion` over the 110 sheets: the same answer as main on all of them.
- A first journey run failed `python-docs-search-results` (`Limit("computed-nodes")`): the scan flag said "motion" for a block with a comment in front of a name, which armed the motion code and made extra style reads. Fixed: comments are skipped, and `has_motion` reads the flagged blocks. Test: `has_motion_is_the_same_for_a_block_that_is_not_read`.

### Numbers

Machine: archMachine, load average 8 to 12 from other agents. Instruction counts hold under load. Wall time does not.

- `bare-bench` (wall ms, 3 runs, main / now): css tokenize 41.7 to 45.2 / 23.3 to 24.0; css parse 85.9 to 90.7 / 67.8 to 70.5; `add 10,000 rules` 11.6 to 26.3 / 5.3 to 5.7. Memory of that row 7.3 MB / 7.8 MB.
- Journeys, after the rebase on main `226935a5` (`tools/bench/journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`, corpus `virtual`, 47 journeys, all pass, same-binary spread at most 0.5%): instructions, sum of medians 96,300 M / 93,856 M, -2.5%. CPU -2.7%, wall -2.5%, PSS sum 1,555.8 / 1,542.9 MiB (-0.8%), peak RSS +0.3%. No journey is over +0.5%. Largest: `docs-rs-home` -32.6%, `duckduckgo-html-search` -24.0%, `rust-lang-org-home` -18.8%, `python-org-docs-link` -16.0%, `python-org-search` -15.9%, `example-learn-more` -13.4%. JS-bound journeys (`react-docs`, `rust-book-search`) do not move.
- Journeys before the virtual clock existed (real clock, main `fe2d54cd`, 3 runs): the 34 journeys with under 3% spread: -4.7%. The `python-docs-search-results` journey failed on this build in the first run (see Exactness, fixed).
- `bare-stress scale css` (MB at the middle size, main / now): `css-rules` 433 / 450, `css-declarations` 63 / 73, `css-important` 31.5 / 41.5, `css-bad-rules` 151 / 162. Time at the middle size: `css-rules` 719 to 1021 ms / 390 to 422 ms, `css-bad-rules` 445 to 473 ms / 310 to 336 ms.
- The target of about 250 B per rule on `css-rules` is not met. Memory went up by 10 to 17 B per rule. The retained sheet text and the `Body` record (24 bytes) cost more than the declarations that the old parse kept for a block of one declaration (`.a{color:red}`). The selector of each rule is the larger part of the 433 B, and it is parsed at once, as the design says. The journeys show no memory saving either (PSS +0.6%). To do: a smaller selector (agent 4a's area).

### Checks

- `cargo test --release --workspace`: all pass except 2 tests that also fail on main (`downloads::run::tests::a_changed_file_starts_again_from_zero`, 18 of 40 runs on main; `browser_geometry_tests::external_sheets_embedded_sheets_and_inline_styles_cascade_in_order`, 1 of 40 on main, 1 of 15 here) and the `*_openssl` groups listed above.
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` (main `fe2d54cd` vs now): 803 rows, mean change glibc -0.756%, 0 rows over the limit. `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` fail to run, as on main.

### Not tested

- Cascade results of a whole page, lazy against eager, apart from the cascade unit tests and the journeys.
- Wall time on an idle machine.
- A sheet with 64 or more nested blocks in a rule (the scanner bails out; not measured).
- crates/js was not changed, so test262 and exec_diff were not run.
## 2026-11-14: lazy function bodies and regex literals compiled at first use (JS phase P1)

Spec: `docs/design-js.md` P1 (sections 2.3, 2.4, 6.5, 6.6), `docs/design-review.md` section 1. Branch `t3/lazy-js-parse-regex`, on `b6ec7df9`.

### What changed

- The parser parses a long function body fully (so every early error stays), then drops its nodes and keeps a `LazyFn` (`Body::Lazy`). The first call of the function parses it again, with its parameters, into a tree of its own. The tree runs as one more script slot, in the scope that held the stub.
- The tree of a lazy function sits in `LazyFn.parsed`. The cross-realm parse cache keeps the outer program, so all realms of a thread share one parse of each called function. Each realm walks it once.
- Which functions are lazy: a body of 128 bytes or more, in a source of 16 KiB or more, of a plain function, method, getter or setter. Never lazy: arrows, async functions, generators, anything in a class body, a body with `super` or `new.target`, and a function that is called at once (`(function(){...})()`, `!function(){...}()`). The facts that cross the boundary (`arguments`, `this`, `super`, `new.target`, class context) are the reason.
- Limits. The nodes of a loaded function count in `script_nodes`. The second parse counts in `lazy_work`. Both are bound by `max_script_nodes`. A lazy tree does not count toward `max_scripts`. The first parse still counts every node, so a body that is too large still fails at load.
- Regex. The parser checks every literal (`Regex::check`: flags, length, pattern grammar), also in a dropped body. A bad pattern is `Unsupported`, as before. The program is compiled when the literal is first evaluated, and shared by pattern and flags across the realms of the thread (`LIT_PROGRAMS`, at most 2048 programs).
- The bytecode does not run a lazy function. It stays on the tree walker.

### Parse cache

Measured with a temporary counter on the journeys: 24.9% of the scripts that a realm parsed were a hit, 15.8% of the source bytes. Lazy bodies are safe to share: the lazy tree is immutable and owned by the cached program.

### Numbers

Machine archMachine, live sites (the step-1 corpus is not on main), `perf stat -e instructions:u`, 3 runs, minimum. BASE `b6ec7df9`, NEW this branch. The same page gives runs that differ by up to 25%, so a row under about 10% is noise.

Syntax tree size, same binary, lazy on and off (one run each, exact for that run):

| Journey | scripts | nodes eager | nodes lazy | tree bytes eager | tree bytes lazy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `github-docs-home` | 15 | 533,615 | 251,856 | 13.8 MB | 6.7 MB |
| `nextjs-docs` | 141 | 530,693 | 132,369 | 13.7 MB | 3.5 MB |
| `rust-book-search` | 17 | 33,976 | 5,656 | 0.90 MB | 0.16 MB |
| `python-docs-search-results` | 25 | 591,883 | 586,694 | 16.5 MB | 16.4 MB |

Called functions: `github-docs-home` 58 of 1,089 lazy functions, `nextjs-docs` 28 of 1,308, `python-docs-search-results` 15 of 17.

All 46 journeys that pass on both trees (without `duckduckgo-html-search`; `hn-*` fail on both trees in this run, a site block):

| | BASE | NEW |
| --- | --- | --- |
| instructions, sum of minimums | 27,636 M | 27,673 M (+0.14%) |
| peak RSS, sum of minimums | 1,124 MiB | 1,115 MiB (-0.75%) |

The total is inside the noise. The rows that moved most: `nodejs-org-home` 635 to 525 M (-17%) and 28.4 to 22.7 MiB (-20%). `github-docs-home` RSS 55.2 to 56.5 MiB in this set, and 59 to 56 MiB in a same-binary lazy-versus-eager set (3 runs each). The named journeys, instructions M / RSS MiB: `python-docs-search-results` 2,910 / 105.4 to 2,916 / 105.6; `rust-book-search` 4,634 / 96.0 to 4,711 / 95.5; `github-docs-home` 1,503 / 55.2 to 1,533 / 56.5; `nextjs-docs` 1,136 / 30.4 to 1,211 / 32.0.

Success criterion 6 (`python-docs-search-results` peak RSS -20%): this step gives about 0 of it. The 16.4 MB of tree on that journey is one data literal (586,694 nodes in 17 lazy functions). No function body is in it. Hypothesis: a data literal needs its own design (parse it to values, or keep it as text and parse at first use). This is a lever for a later step. Peak RSS of the tree also does not drop by the full tree saving on `github-docs-home` (7 MB less tree, 3 MiB less peak). Hypothesis: the peak is at another point of the run.

### Cost matrix

`tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` against `b6ec7df9`, 803 rows: mean glibc +0.037%, jemalloc +0.355%. One row is over the limit under both allocators: `scripts_load many 10` (+0.90% glibc, +0.51% jemalloc; 0.65 M instructions of 71.7 M, one more word to swap and one more allocation for each of many tiny scripts). 4 rows are over under one allocator only. `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` do not run (known stack size issue).
The first matrix of this branch had 74 rows over the limit (up to +12%). Cause: the table of lazy functions was swapped with each cross-script call, and the `Program` grew. The tables moved out of the swap, and small scripts stay eager. After the change 5 rows are over under one or both allocators.

### Checks

- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: all pass except 7 TLS tests (`bare-net` `https_openssl` 2, `bare-tls` `client_openssl` 4 and `tls12_openssl` 1), as on main.
- `tools/js/test262_check.sh`: gate ok, no directory below the baseline. The first run (every source of 512 bytes or more lazy) and the last run (16 KiB or more) both pass. Test262 files are small, so the last run keeps them eager.
- `tools/js/exec_diff.sh`: 0 differences in 79 runs (tree, auto, byte). It found two bugs in the first version (scope tables of the bytecode). They have tests now.
- New tests: `parse_lazy_tests.rs` (8), `eval_lazy_tests.rs` (13: closures, recursion, constructors, nested lazy functions, early errors, bad regex in a dropped body, limits, two realms, frame slots of functions loaded in turn, the three exec modes on the proxy corpus). `parse_tests::regexp_pattern_gate` and two `eval_builtins_tests` changed: a bad pattern fails at parse time, with the same message and span.
- Two bugs were found by journeys, not by the unit tests: the re-parse of a lazy function made its own body lazy again (found by a test), and the frame layout of one lazy function took the scopes of the next one (found on `rust-book-search`; `lazy_functions_loaded_one_after_the_other_keep_their_own_frame_slots` passes with and without the fix, so it does not guard it).

### Not tested

A script of 16 KiB or more that uses `super`, `new.target`, generators or classes together with lazy functions beyond the corpus fixtures. The byte lane with a lazy function inside a class (not lazy by rule). Windows and macOS. Memory at the end of a long run (the lazy trees live as long as the cached program, bound by `parse_cache::MAX_BYTES`). `keycost.sh` (no change on the typing path).

### Noticed, not changed

- An `Unsupported` error inside a lazy body (for example a feature that the evaluator refuses) shows at the first call, not at load. A `CompileError::Limit` of the regex emit pass shows at the first evaluation of the literal, not at load.
- Arrows are the largest group of functions that stay eager. A later step can make them lazy once the lexical `this` and `arguments` cross the boundary.
- `rust-book-search` loads 191 lazy functions (its scripts hold 144 at the top level; the others sit inside lazy trees). 19,850 nodes of its 33,976 are parsed twice. A script where most functions run pays about two parses for them.
- The parse cache keeps a separate entry for the lazy and the eager kind of the same text.
