## 2026-11-13: ancestor-keyed rule lists and a restyle charge for real work (step 4, phase 2)

Design: `design-style.md` section 3.1 (M2), 3.3 (I4, I5) and 4.2. Branch `t3/ancestor-bucket-indexing`, rebased on `e6b3f707`.

### What changed

- A rule list with more than 16 entries (`SPLIT_FROM`) gets a second level. Each rule goes under the rarest hash of its mandatory ancestors: the tags, ids and classes that a descendant or child combinator needs. A rule with no such hash goes to a `rest` list. The layout is flat: `keys` (sorted), `starts`, `list`, `rest`; one `Big` for each list. It is made once, at the first look-up after a rule is added (`Index::bigs`). It covers the id, class, tag and attribute lists and the `other` list.
- An element reads `rest` and the groups of the hashes on its path. The ancestor filter now also keeps its path: the distinct hashes with a count, exact. The look-up takes the shorter of two ways: the keys through the Bloom filter, or the path hashes through a binary search of the keys. Source order and specificity order are not changed: the fuzz compares the matched lists with the old path.
- The path is kept only when some list has a split (`AncestorFilter::track`). The loop of a full compute has the flag as a const generic, so a page with no split pays no test in the loop.
- `RuleSet::styled_elements()` is new. The restyle charge is `STEPS_PER_RESTYLED_ELEMENT` (64 before, 32 now) for each element that `RuleSet::restyle` styled, plus its tested candidates and the look-ups. The estimate loop (`visited`, `changed_roots`, `elements_under`) is gone from `restyle_marks`.
- `#[inline]` on `browser_dataset::matches`: see "Cost gate" below. It is not a change of behaviour.

### Why 32 steps

A step is about 200 instructions (26 ns). A restyle costs 6,500 to 7,200 instructions for each element with 8 candidates (probe on `rest_13` and `compm_22000`: 39 M for 6,002 elements, 315 M for 44,002). That is 33 to 36 steps, candidates included. `rest_13` charges 6,002 x 32 + 51,001 = 243 K steps for each restyle. The real cost is about 195 K steps (1.25 times). The old charge was about 35 M steps for a real cost of 3.9 M (9 to 10 times).

### Numbers

Machine archMachine, instructions of `perf stat -e instructions:u`, 3 runs, the spread is under 0.001 G on every row. BASE `f6415364`, MAIN `e6b3f707` (has none of this), BRANCH this branch. Pages from `/data/bare-tmp/bm/b/pages`, steps `run.steps`. "limit" is the drive result `ok=false`.

| Page | BASE | MAIN | BRANCH | BASE / BRANCH |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `compm_2000` | 0.248 G | 0.248 G | 0.176 G | 1.4 |
| `compm_8000` | 1.953 G | 1.953 G | 0.687 G | 2.8 |
| `compm_22000` | 11.664 G | 11.664 G | 1.898 G | 6.1 |
| `rest_2` | 2.178 G | 2.178 G | 0.729 G | 3.0 |
| `rest_13` | 10.873 G | 10.873 G | 1.403 G | 7.7 |
| `rest_30` | 11.636 G, Steps limit | 11.636 G, Steps limit | 2.443 G, passes | |
| `rest_50` | 11.636 G, Steps limit | 11.636 G, Steps limit | 3.668 G, passes | |
| `comp_8000` | 0.234 G | 0.234 G | 0.233 G | 1.0 |
| `comp_16000` | 0.466 G | 0.466 G | 0.463 G | 1.0 |

The growth exponent of `compm` (instructions against the size): BASE 1.61 from 2,000 to 22,000 (1.76 from 8,000 to 22,000); BRANCH 0.99 (1.00 from 8,000 to 22,000). Each added restyle in the `rest` ramp costs 0.79 G on BASE and 61 M on BRANCH (12.9 times less). The `comp` pages have few rules, so they were never quadratic.

**Criterion 3 (10 times lower on `compm_22000` and `rest_13`) is not met: 6.1 and 7.7 times.** The matching is now linear and a restyle pass is 12.9 times cheaper, but a part of the page cost is not matching:
- A fixed cost of about 0.6 G (the page parse, the parse of 36,000 rules, the index build). It belongs to phase 4 (lazy rule bodies, faster tokenizer). `rest_2` shows it: 0.73 G.
- The cascade of the matched lists that are unique: `hash_values`, `ComputedStyle` equality and the dedupe. One `compute_kept` of `compm_22000` takes 536 M instructions for 44,002 elements, with 8 candidates for each element (351,930 tested). That is not matching.
Hypothesis: with phase 4 done, `rest_13` falls to about 0.9 G (12 times). Not measured.

### The limits

- The restyle charge now matches the cost (criterion 8, first half). `rest_30` and `rest_50` end with the Steps limit on BASE and MAIN and pass on BRANCH.
- `computed-work` (nodes times rules, or styled elements times rules) is kept, unchanged. It bounds one full compute, which cannot be interrupted, and the real work of the compute is still not bounded by the index: a list that stays whole (a rule with no ancestor, or many rules with the same key, like `html span`) gives elements x rules candidates. `css-same-class 20000` (20,000 elements, 20,000 rules `.a`) is 101.3 G instructions on BASE and BRANCH. The cap still refuses `comp_48000` and `compm_34000` on BRANCH, although the index makes them cheap. With the cap at 2^60 (one build of BASE and one of an earlier BRANCH): `comp_48000` 1.39 G on both; `compm_30000` BASE 14.2 G and Steps limit, BRANCH 2.42 G and passes; `compm_34000` BASE 18.2 G and Steps limit, BRANCH 2.98 G and passes. So the cap refuses pages that cost 1 to 3 G. A cap by the real work needs the compute to count candidates and stop. That is `sources_capped` in `cascade.rs`, which another task is changing. The cap is not changed here.
- The 65,536 cap of `cssom-objects` is not part of this task.

### Journeys

The corpus of step 1 is on `t3/repeatable-journey-benchmarks` (`tools/bench`, not on main). I built that branch (`cc8cd9d0`) once with and once without this change and replayed the corpus with `journeys.sh compare --runs 3`. `nextjs-docs` is not in the corpus (it did not pass when recorded). All 47 pass on both.

The sum of the medians moves by more than the change, because some journeys are not stable from run to run on the same binary (for example `rust-book-search`: 3.9 G to 13.7 G with no split at all; `wikipedia-search`, `mdn-reference`, `nodejs-org-home`). First compare (threshold 16): 76,244 to 74,900 M (-1.8%). Last compare (final code): 75,360 to 76,702 M (+1.8%). Over the 37 journeys whose spread is under 3% on both binaries: 37,071 to 37,139 M (+0.18%). I did not find a gain on the journeys. They have no long rule list with ancestor keys that the index could cut, except the noisy ones. The long-tail journeys `python-org-docs-link` (-0.4%) and `python-org-search` (-0.3%) did not move. Criterion 4 (1.3 times on the sheet-scan journeys) is therefore not shown by this change: `rust-book-search` cannot be read through its spread of 190%.

Threshold: with `BARE_SPLIT_FROM` (a temporary switch, removed) at never, 8, 16, 32 and 64, the 23 stable journeys sum to 18,380 / 18,453 / 18,489 / 18,471 / 18,403 M (BASE 18,397 M). No threshold costs or gains more than 0.5%. 16 stays, the start value of the task.

### Cost gate (`tools/js/cost_matrix.sh`, against `e6b3f707`)

803 rows. First build: 124 rows over +0.5% under both allocators (the worst +4.1%, `block-deep-over-limit 20000`). Cause: about 90 instructions for each element in `Index::collect` (a call to `bigs` and an indirect call for each list) and in the filter. Fixes: `bigs` is one inlined test, and the common path is the old code (`gather::<false>`); the split path is a separate function; the `track` flag is a const generic in the loop of a full compute. Last build: 0 rows over under both; 3 rows over under glibc only (`block-deep 40`, `block-nested-collapse 20`, `overflow-nested-auto 20`, +0.51% to +0.54%, under jemalloc +0.13%). Mean change glibc +0.019%, jemalloc +0.131%. 2 rows (`parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`) do not run on either tree.

`examples/dataset_load keys 1000 50` and `10000 50` were +0.6% under both allocators. Bisect: they are JS rows that never run a cascade. With the `browser_computed.rs` of MAIN and the `cascade.rs` of this branch the count is the same as MAIN (336.87 M). With the `browser_computed.rs` of this branch it is +2.0 M. The loop in `browser_dataset::matches` is compiled in a different way. `#[inline]` on `matches` gives 336.77 M (-0.03%) and the rows pass. It is one attribute in a file that this task does not otherwise touch.

### Rebase on `e497ff5f` (lazy CSS bodies, #498) and the `sheets_load dynamic` row

The rebase had one conflict, in `cascade.rs`. Main's lazy bodies were kept; this branch added the `styled` field and `ancestor_hashes(&selector, false)` in `push`. After it, `examples/sheets_load dynamic 10` was +1.09% (glibc) and +0.98% (jemalloc); `dynamic 1` was +0.49%. Cause: `Index::make_bigs` ran at the first look-up after each `push`, and scanned every key of the four bucket maps to find a list over `split_from`. `dynamic` adds 50 sheets, one `#dN` rule each, so the rule set is rebuilt 50 times with up to 50 id buckets: a scan of all keys at each rebuild, and no list is over 16. IBS profile (6 runs): `OnceCell::try_init`, `HashMap::extend` and `cfree` were the new samples. Fix: `Index::push` keeps `longest`, the length of the longest list. `make_bigs` returns `None` at once when `longest <= split_from`, so a rule set with no long list pays no scan, whatever its number of keys. The scan stays only for a set that has a long list, and the split costs more than the scan there. Not a change for this benchmark: any page that adds sheets or rules one by one has the same cost.

Numbers (`tools/js/instr.sh`, minimum of 3, same machine): `sheets_load dynamic 10` main 48.59 M, branch 48.76 M (+0.36%, two A/B pairs: +0.37%, +0.34%); before the fix 49.13 M (+1.1%). Full matrix against main `e497ff5f`: 803 rows, 0 over +0.5% under both allocators; 14 over under glibc only (`bare-stress` block and inline rows, +0.5% to +0.9%, jemalloc +0.16% to +0.46%). Mean glibc +0.035%, jemalloc +0.200%. 2 rows (`parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`) do not run on either tree (stack overflow, same on main). Ramps, `bare-drive`, 3 runs: `compm_22000` 1.834 G (spread 0.005 G), `rest_13` 1.241 G (spread 0.001 G); peak RSS 71 to 72 MiB and 55 MiB. `bare-css` lib 261 pass, `bare` lib 1436 pass.

### Memory

`bare-stress scale css` (BASE and BRANCH): the same peak MB on `css-class-index` (138.1 MB at 200,000), `css-same-class` (10.7 MB), `css-import-many`. Instructions of `css-same-class 20000`: 101.29 G on both; `css-class-index 200000`: 12.10 G and 12.09 G. A first run flagged `css-same-class` and `css-class-index` as timeouts on BRANCH; the machine was loaded, the second run flagged none and the instructions are equal.
Index size, measured with a counting allocator on the sheets of `compm_22000`, `compm_8000` and `rest_13` (a one-element page, `RuleSet::compute`): 4.2 to 4.9 B for each rule stays after the compute (`keys`, `starts`, `list`, `rest`). The peak during the build of the split is 18.0 to 19.5 B for each rule (the hashes of the rules, the frequency map, the sorted pairs). It is freed at once. Both are inside the budget of 20 B for each rule.
Peak RSS of the ramps: `compm_22000` 68 to 69 MiB, `rest_13` 52 to 53 MiB (BASE 68 and 52).

### Checks

- `cargo test --release -p bare-css --lib`: 256 pass. `cargo test --release -p bare --lib browser_computed`: 41 pass, 1 ignored.
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: all pass except 7 TLS tests (`bare-net` `https_openssl` 2, `bare-tls` `client_openssl` 4 and `tls12_openssl` 1). They fail the same way on main (the openssl of this machine, see the section above).
- New file `crates/css/src/cascade/index_tests.rs`. A differential fuzz: random trees, random sheets (`:is()`, `:not()`, `:has()`, sibling combinators, child and descendant paths, repeated classes), with the split threshold at never, 0, 1, 2 and 5. The matched list with the split equals the matched list of the old path (all entries of the bucket, with the Bloom check and `matches`), and every true match is a candidate. 400 cases, over 100 sheets have a split. Also: a sibling of an ancestor is not a key; 200 nested divs; a filter counter that is saturated (300 ancestors with one class); shadow trees (150 cases, the style of each node is the same for all thresholds); `restyle` against a new `compute` (150 cases). Mutation checks: keys from the old hashes make the fuzz fail ("rule N matches element M and is not offered").
- New test `thirty_restyles_of_a_page_with_a_long_tag_list_fit_the_step_budget` (3,000 divs and spans, 18,000 rules `.kN span`, 30 restyles under the default limits). I did not run it on BASE; by the model of the old charge it fails there.
- `a_read_after_a_change_charges_the_elements_it_restyles` now runs 120 restyles (60 before): the charge is half.

### Not tested

`test262_check.sh` and `exec_diff.sh` (no change in `crates/js`). Window mode. Pages with shadow trees on a real site (only the fuzz and the unit tests). The journeys on the final code against main `e6b3f707` itself (the corpus runner is not on main; the compare is on `cc8cd9d0` with and without this change). Peak RSS on journeys. The new test against BASE.

### Noticed, not changed

- The old ancestor filter takes `.a` of `.a ~ .b > .c` as an ancestor, although `.a` is a sibling of the parent. The filter then rejects the rule for every element. Chrome does not (to verify). `rust-book-chapters` depends on it: with the rule fixed, `#mdbook-sidebar-toggle-anchor:checked ~ .page-wrapper .nav-wide-wrapper {display:none}` (in `@media (max-width:1380px)`) matches, `a.nav-chapters.next` is hidden and the journey fails. The Bloom hashes keep the old rule, so the styles are the same. The split keys use the exact ancestors.
- The index offers a class list twice for an element that repeats a class token (`class="e e a"`). The matcher gives the same rule twice then (the fuzz compares the lists without the repeats).
- The candidates of a shadow tree index are not counted in `tested`.
- `restyle` allocates a 4 KiB filter for each root.
- A list that stays whole (a rule with no ancestor, or many rules with the same key) is still elements x rules. `computed-work` guards that case.
- The Bloom filter and the exact path are two structures for one set. One structure with a count for each hash would do both; it needs a hash table for the path.

## 2026-11-14: large data literals are kept as source text; lazy arrow functions measured and not shipped (step 8, criterion 6)

Task: lower the peak RSS of `python-docs-search-results` by 20% or more (criterion 6) with lazy arrow functions and a compact store for large data literals. Base: main `5b42d061` (the rebase target). Machine: archMachine, shared. Journeys: `tools/bench/journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`, corpus `virtual`, both binaries built with `--release --workspace --examples`. The virtual clock makes the work the same in each run, so the instruction spread is 0.0%.

### What was built

- `ExprKind::Data` (`crates/js/src/data_lit.rs`). The parser checks an array or object literal with `data_lit::scan`. The literal must be JSON in script text: double-quoted strings with JSON escapes, JSON numbers, `true`, `false`, `null`, string keys, JSON white space only, depth 64 or less, and no key `__proto__` (also when an escape spells it). The literal must have 128 bytes or more. Then the literal is one node: its span. The lexer jumps over the text (`Lexer::seek`).
- The evaluator builds the heap values from the text (`data_lit::build`): `intern_str` for strings, `define_own_property` for keys, `Heap::fill_array` for arrays, an integer path for numbers of 15 digits or less and `number::decimal_value` for the rest. It does not make the tree walk that the same literal makes, and it does not allocate a node for each value.
- Only a source of 16 KiB or more has data nodes (the lazy kind of the parse cache). Smaller sources keep every literal as a tree, so test262 and the other short scripts do not use the new path.
- A literal with code inside (`[f(), [1,2,...]]`) stays a tree. Its large plain parts are data nodes.
- Observable values are those of the tree walk: property order, `-0`, `1e400`, numeric keys, duplicate keys, lone surrogates, `length` and `constructor` keys. `data_lit_tests.rs` has 12 tests, most of them differential: the same literal in a short source (tree) and a padded source (text) must give the same dump of prototype, key order, attributes and the sign of zero.
- V8 comparison: V8 keeps boilerplates (`CreateObjectLiteral` makes them from constant data) and its guidance for a large literal is `JSON.parse` (<https://v8.dev/blog/cost-of-javascript-2019>). We copied the idea (a large literal of constants is data, not code). We copied no code. Our design keeps the source span as the only record, so the cost of a literal in memory is the text that the page already holds.
- Other choices (see `docs/decisions.md`): a flat node table (a smaller tree, still 8 to 12 bytes for each value) and the generic `json.rs` parser (it makes a different property list for `__proto__`).

### Numbers (base `5b42d061`, median of runs 1 to 3)

| Journey | Minstr base | Minstr new | change | MiB base | MiB new | change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| python-docs-search-results | 3377.9 | 2539.6 | -24.8% | 114.5 | 91.2 | -20.4% |
| python-docs-search | 2138.2 | 1300.5 | -39.2% | 93.8 | 68.1 | -27.5% |
| rust-book-search | 16559.5 | 16418.0 | -0.9% | 129.6 | 129.4 | -0.1% |
| 47 journeys, sum of medians | 92654.7 | 90256.9 | -2.6% | 1737.3 | 1671.5 | -3.8% |

- Criterion 6: `python-docs-search-results` peak RSS 114.5 to 91.2 MiB (-20.4%). The criterion baseline is 116 MiB, so the target is 92.8 MiB or lower. The three runs are 93, 91 and 90 MiB (a spread of 3%, from the allocator). The peak of PSS (run 0): 103.9 to 90.6 MiB (-12.8%). The target is met on the median, not by a wide margin.
- Instruction spread: at most 0.6% (base) and 0.2% (new) over all journeys. No journey grew by 0.3% or more in instructions. Peak RSS moves by up to 3% between builds and runs (`go-dev-home` +3.1%, `github-docs-home` -2.8%).
- Same source, other build: a `-p bare-drive` build and a `--workspace --examples` build of the same commit differ by 2.5% instructions on `github-docs-home` (the difference is in `bare_css::matching::compound_matches` and `scan::rule`, which this change does not touch). Compare only binaries that were built the same way as the base.
- Threshold. A script of 16 KiB with one literal of about N bytes, a new realm for each run, instructions of the whole process divided by the runs (`tools/js/instr.sh`, minimum of 3). The tree column has the first key unquoted, which makes the same literal a tree. A script without the literal costs 1.784 M.

  | N (bytes) | run once: text | run once: tree | called 100 times in a function: text | tree |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 64 | 1.803 M | 1.836 M | 3.209 M | 3.316 M |
  | 128 | 1.811 M | 1.861 M | 3.853 M | 3.946 M |
  | 256 | 1.834 M | 1.934 M | 5.416 M | 5.660 M |
  | 512 | 1.874 M | 2.053 M | 8.075 M | 8.453 M |
  | 1024 | 1.953 M | 2.291 M | 13.417 M | 14.019 M |
  | 2048 | 2.109 M | 2.762 M | | |
  | 8192 | 3.038 M | 5.537 M | | |
  | 65536 | 11.50 M | 30.75 M | | |

  The text path costs less than the tree from 64 bytes up, also for a literal that a function builds 100 times. The gain grows with the size (`65536` bytes: 2.7 times). The threshold is 128 bytes: it is the first size where one literal saves more than 2% of the script. The first choice, 1024, was a guess; the table shows that it left the small literals out for no reason.
- `max_script_nodes` counts a data literal as one node, so the node limit does not guard the size of a literal any more. The heap limits do (`HeapError` at the first value that does not fit; a test covers it). No limit was removed.

### Lazy arrow functions: built, measured, not shipped

The arrow work is on the branch `t3/lazy-arrows-experiment` (commit `6c4a4185`, based on `e497ff5f`), not in this change. It makes an arrow with a plain parameter list and a body of 128 bytes or more lazy by the rules of #492, plus a fact `arguments` (an arrow reads `arguments` of the function around it) and a start mark for the function that is parsed again. It has parse tests and run tests (this, closures, recursion, currying, `arguments`, `new.target`, `super`, async, class fields, early errors, three exec modes) and passes them.

Measured against the same tree without lazy arrows (both built with `-p bare-drive`, 3 runs, 0.0% spread):

| Journey | instructions with lazy arrows | peak RSS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| github-docs-home | +3.95% (4911 to 5105 M) | -1.8% |
| nodejs-org-home | +2.24% | -0.7% |
| react-docs | +1.29% | +0.3% |
| python-docs-search | +0.76% | -0.5% |
| python-docs-search-results | +0.41% | -0.5% |
| 47 journeys | total -1.7% against -2.3% without lazy arrows | -2.7% against -3.2% |

- Cause (measured by a counter in the parser and in `parse_lazy_function`): on `github-docs-home` 68 arrows were made lazy (1.22 MB of body text, nested ones counted at each level) and 51 of them ran (1.16 MB parsed a second time). The largest ones are 283, 175 and 133 KB: module factories of a bundle, called once at load. A function that runs pays two parses and saves no memory, because the tree of a called function stays in its own slot. Hypothesis: the second parse costs 167 instructions for each byte (194 M for 1.16 MB, the size of the difference).
- Sizes that were tried (all on `github-docs-home`, instructions against the base): a minimum body of 512 bytes +3.7%, of 2048 bytes +3.3%; a maximum body of 4096 bytes +0.9%, of 16384 bytes +1.5%, of 65536 bytes +2.4%. No size removes the cost. No journey of the corpus holds memory in arrows that never run.
- Decision: arrows stay eager. `scripts_load many 10` (the #492 exception) is not helped either: its scripts are smaller than 16 KiB.
- The data path alone gives the whole gain for criterion 6: `python-docs-search-results` with and without lazy arrows differs by 0.5% RSS (with lazy arrows it is the higher one).

### The double parse on `rust-book-search`

`rust-book-search` has 456 lazy function bodies (560 KB of text) and 12 lazy arrows in the experiment (4.6 KB). 166 functions run (326 KB parsed a second time). So the double parse is the cost of a lazy function that runs (the design of #492), and arrows are not part of it. Estimated cost: 326 KB at about 167 instructions for each byte is 55 M, 0.3% of the 16.4 G of the journey (hypothesis: the 167 comes from the `github-docs-home` row above). It is not a large part of this journey. Not changed. A cheaper first parse (a preparser without tree nodes) would be the design change that removes this kind of cost; this task did not include it.

### Checks

- `cargo test --release -p bare-js --lib`: 930 passed, 1 ignored.
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: all pass except the 7 TLS tests that fail on main (`bare-net` `https_openssl` 2, `bare-tls` `client_openssl` 4 and `tls12_openssl` 1). `a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved` (`bare-mcp`) failed once under load and passed alone.
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` against `5b42d061`: 803 rows, mean glibc -0.011%, 0 rows over the limit, 2 rows did not run (`parse_load deep 1`, `deep 10`: the stack size issue that earlier entries list).
- `TEST262=/data/claude-tmp/test262 tools/js/test262_check.sh`: gate ok (29731 pass).
- `tools/js/exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, tree, auto and byte, 0 differences.
- `tools/js/typing/keycost.sh`: 294.2 M for each key on `#a1` (base 294.19 M), load and mount 618.6 M (base 618 M), peak RSS 33.9 MiB at 50 keys.

### Not tested

A data literal in a module source (`ModuleLazy`; the tests use classic scripts). Windows and macOS. Memory at the end of a long run. A page whose data literal is invalid JSON only at its end (the scan gives up and the tree is built; a test covers the grammar, not a large literal that fails at the last byte). The lazy arrow branch on the whole workspace test run and on test262 (its crate tests pass; the gates ran on this change only).

### Noticed, not changed

- A `super` call in an arrow inside an object-literal method gives `Unsupported "super outside a class element"` in the eager run (found while writing an arrow test on the experiment branch; not run on main).
- Most tests of `eval_lazy_tests.rs` run on a source below 16 KiB, so they run the eager path. Only a padded source (a comment of 16 KiB) runs lazy functions.
- On the experiment branch an arrow in parentheses that starts a call, `(() => ...)()`, was lazy at first, because the inner `(` moves `eager_at` before the arrow is checked. A test caught it. It matters only if arrows become lazy.
- `rust-book-search` is 0.9% lower in instructions with this change. The cause was not examined.
## Rule-set sharing: measurements and design (docs only)

Design: `docs/design-rule-share.md`. Nothing is built. Main `5b42d061`, archMachine (shared, load 6 to 22). Instructions are `instructions:u`. Totals are 3 runs; the phase split comes from temporary counters (1 run each, not in the repository) and `force_count.py` agrees on the suite.

### Hypothesis verdict

The rule set and its index are built again for each document: confirmed. The parsed sheet is cached: rejected. There is no CSS parse cache. The tokenizer and the selector parse run in every build and are 73% of it.

### Share of the build

| Workload | Total (3 runs) | Build | Build, split lists, body reads |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Suite, V2, one worker | 13,101 M (13,099 to 13,103) | 2,134 M (16.3%), 191 builds, 11.17 M each | 2,368 M (18.1%) |
| 47 corpus journeys | 92,643 M (92,434 to 92,643) | 2,005 M (2.16%), 140 builds, 94 documents | 2,421 M (2.61%) |
| `compm_22000` | 1,834 M (spread 0.1 M) | 111.6 M (6.1%), 1 build | 156.5 M (8.5%) |
| `rest_13` | 1,241 M (spread 0.0 M) | 180.5 M (14.5%), 1 build | 214.6 M (17.3%) |

The step 6 shares (30.9% suite, 7.8 to 8.3% journeys) are lower today. Hypothesis: lazy bodies (#498). I did not run the old commit. The "0.6 G fixed cost" of the ramps is not the build (`rest_2` costs 580 M, the build 215 M).

Split of the suite build: selector parse 51% (2,690 per selector), tokenizer and text copy 22%, index push 12% (590 per entry), entry and the rest 11%, body step 4%.

### Repeats

- Suite: 1 distinct sheet list in 191 builds. 190 builds repeat (99.5% of the build).
- Journeys: 41 of 140 builds repeat a whole earlier list (338 M, 0.36% of all instructions); 24 of 47 journeys have one. 41 builds are full rebuilds inside one document (a late `<link>` or an edited `<style>` breaks `starts_with`). 63% of the build instructions are in a sheet that an earlier build had (890 M in the same document, 316 M in an earlier document, 51 M the UA sheet).
- Ramps: one document, one build. No repeat.

### Recommendation and expected gain (estimates, not built)

Process-wide name atoms first, then a cache of immutable `Rc<RuleSet>` keyed by the sheet list and the viewport. A per-sheet parse cache only if a gate says so. Suite V2 13.1 to about 10.75 G (criterion 7: 1.97 times against the frozen V0, 1.69 times against V0 of the same binary; now 1.62 and 1.38). Journeys -0.4% (all sharing together at most 1.6%). Ramps: no change. A cheaper first selector parse is the only lever on the ramps (hypothesis: `rest_13` 9.3 times, `compm_22000` 6.5 times) and is a separate design.

### Not tested

Nothing was built, so no cost matrix, test262 or workspace test ran. Wall time. The live size of a rule set. The cost of a process-wide `intern`. The hit rate on a real warm suite. Details in section 7 of the design document.
## JS strings: atoms, flat strings and ropes (2026-11-14, `docs/design-js.md` phase P2)

Status: built and tested. **Not merged.** The first build broke the cost rule on 426 of 803 rows. The cost fix (below) leaves 12 rows over +0.5% under both allocators (largest +0.93%). The cost rule is still broken, so the owner decides.

### What changed

- A string is one of three kinds. `StrId.index` bit 31 (`STR_ROPE`) tells a rope. `StrId.gn` bit 31 (`GN_ATOM`) tells an atom. The slab keeps that bit in the generation of the slot (`Slab::tag`). Flat string: no bit. The rope has its own slab (`Heap::ropes`).
- Atom: interned. One atom for each content. `ATOM_MAX` is 32 code units. Every string of 32 units or fewer is an atom.
- Flat string: more than 32 units, not interned. No hash, no table probe, one allocation.
- Rope: the result of `+` or `+=` above 32 units. Node = `{left, right, len, flat: OnceCell<Box<[u16]>>}`. The first read of the units flattens it (iterative, from the end, no recursion). The node then keeps the flat units and the GC does not mark its children.
- `===`: `Heap::str_eq`. Same handle: equal. Two atoms with different handles: not equal. Otherwise compare length, then units. `StrId` has no `PartialEq` and no `Hash`: the compiler found every use. `ByHandle` is the key of a table.
- A property key, a `Map` or `Set` key, a `Symbol.for` key and a regexp cache key is an atom (`atom_of`). `check_key` refuses a non-atom key with `InvalidKey`. Names from the parser use `atom_str` (a long identifier is still a key).
- Size: a rope node is 32 B plus about 12 B of slab slot, about 44 B for each part. The design said 24 B. The `OnceCell` (16 B) is the difference. `Value` is unchanged (16 B).
- `max_bytes` (1 GiB) is the limit that the concat loop hit before (`Limit(Heap(Bytes))` at 100k parts). The loop does not reach it now. No limit was removed or raised: the limit still protects the flat result.

### Ramps (`eval_load concat_n` and `concat_pre_n`, scale = number of parts, one part per step)

Machine archMachine (AMD Zen3), `cargo --release`, one run each, run time from the example. Base = main `fe2d54cd`.

| parts | `s += x` base | `s += x` new | `s = x + s` base | `s = x + s` new | peak RSS base / new |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 1.3 ms | 0.2 ms | 1.4 ms | 0.2 ms | 7.3 / 5.7 MiB |
| 10,000 | 85.6 ms | 2.0 ms | 90.5 ms | 2.0 ms | 196.9 / 6.1 MiB |
| 100,000 | limit (Bytes) | 17.2 ms | limit (Bytes) | 17.1 ms | - / 10.7 MiB |
| 1,000,000 | limit (Bytes) | 169.5 ms | limit (Bytes) | 167.4 ms | - / 56.2 MiB |

New time is linear: 10x parts gives 8.6x to 10x time. Base is quadratic (10x parts gives 66x time, then the limit).

### Cost

First build (base `fe2d54cd`): keycost +0.8% for each key, cost matrix mean +0.85% glibc, 426 of 803 rows over +0.5% under both allocators, journeys +0.55%, setup +120 K instructions.

#### Cause

I used callgrind (`valgrind --tool=callgrind`, per-function and per-instruction diffs of base against new). `perf record` gives too few samples on these short runs. The cost was not one thing. It was the compiler changing its inlining and register choices around the string code:

- Small hot paths were not inlined any more (`check_value`, `check_str`, `str_units`, `str_len`, `code_unit_at`, `strict_equals`, `key_from_string`). Each one then cost a call and a frame.
- A call that can fail inside a loop made the compiler store the iterator and keep more registers.
- A flat read went through two cold calls when the kind was a bit of `index` (+4.6 M on `builtins_load zero`, +10% on some rows).
- Double work: `intern` copied an owned `Vec` (one extra `malloc` and `free` for each `substring`), `+` did two lookups, `lastIndexOf` built its closure for every element.

#### Fix (design, not patches)

- One encoding rule: atoms and flat strings are read by the one old `strings.get(index, gn)`. A rope misses (its index is out of range) and takes a `#[cold] #[inline(never)]` slow path (`units_slow`, `len_slow`, `check_digit_key`, `key_from_other`, `units_eq`, `concat_long`). The common case has one branch and no rope code.
- Tiny fast paths are `#[inline(always)]`. One copy of the intern code (`intern_slice`, `intern_owned`, `insert_atom`): one hash, one probe, one insert. `substring` of 32 units or fewer uses a stack buffer.
- `Interner::rebuild` takes its size from the live count.
- `Str.digit` also means "needs a closer key check" for flat strings, so a key check is one load.

#### Numbers (archMachine, base = main `1306e82a`, new = this branch)

- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh`: 803 rows, mean -0.35% glibc. **12 rows over +0.5% under both allocators**, 2 more over under one only, 2 rows fail on both trees (`parse_load deep 1`, `deep 10`: stack overflow on main too). Rows over (glibc / jemalloc): `wrapper_load forin 10000 30000` +0.93% / +0.87%, `forin 1000 3000` +0.85% / +0.70%, `sc_load custom_iter 10` +0.76% / +0.72%, `gen_load iterobj 10` +0.72% / +0.74%, `gen_load iterobj 1` +0.69% / +0.60%, `iterator_load generic 10` +0.64% / +0.66%, `generic 1` +0.62% / +0.58%, `tagged_load sites 10` +0.60% / +0.60%, `weak_load dead_cycles 10` +0.58% / +0.56%, `iterator_load set_diff 10` +0.57% / +0.56%, `set_sym 10` +0.55% / +0.54%, `arrobj_load tosorted 10` +0.52% / +0.51%.
- `tools/js/typing/keycost.sh`: `#a1` 294.8 M each key (base 294.2 M, +0.2%). `#f0` 300.1 M (base 299.6 M, +0.2%). Load and mount 620.0 M (base 618.6 M, +0.2%). Peak RSS 34.0 MiB at 50 keys (base 33.9 MiB).
- Setup: `eval_load loop 0` 2.79 M (base 2.78 M, +0.14%). It was +120 K.
- Journeys (`tools/bench/journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`, corpus `virtual`, 47 journeys, all pass): sum of medians 90,448 M base, 90,517 M new (+0.1%). Instruction spread at most 0.2%. Two journeys are over +0.5%: `python-docs-search-results` +0.7%, `python-docs-search` +0.6%. PSS and peak RSS sums +0.5% and +0.8%: not stable (single journeys move from -3.5% to +4% in both directions, same as the run to run noise of the page).
- Concat gains kept: the ramp table above is unchanged by the fix.

#### What I tried and dropped (each an A/B of exact counts)

- `extern "C"` string compare: no gain, worse on `arrays`. Manual index loop in `lastIndexOf`: +4.97%. Both reverted.
- `Slab::alloc` split into an always-inline copy for strings: no change.
- Hash of a string key as one `u64`, or without the `GN_ATOM` bit, and a final fold in `Fx`: no gain or worse on `wrapper_load forin` (+1.3% to +2.8%). The hash is not the cause.
- `check_value` as a plain function: worse everywhere (+0.7% on `eval_load loop 0`). `check_value` with the rope test out of line: no gain on `iterator_load generic`, +0.3% on `loop 0`.

#### Open cause (hypothesis)

The 12 rows are object allocation and iterator results (`new_object_with_shape` +23 instructions a call, `member_put` +13) and `for-in` key sets (`HashMap::insert`, `PropMap::find`). In `new_object_with_shape` the inlined `check_value` loop keeps more live pointers (the rope slab is one more) and the compiler hoists and spills them. I did not find a layout that removes this without a cost elsewhere. Two attempts on this cost failed, so I stopped, as the rules say.

### Not built

- The process-wide atom table (design section 6.4, "built once per process for builtin and host names"). A realm would still need the table copied or built lazily, and a `Str` enum for static strings would add 8 B for each string. Estimate: about 0.2% of the instructions of a journey. It would also reduce the +120 K of setup. Left for a later step.
- A different `ATOM_MAX`. The value 32 is the design's value (to tune). I took length counts of strings in a build with counters, then removed the counters. I did not run the journeys with 16 or 64.

### Checks

- `cargo test --release -p bare-js --lib`: all pass. New tests: `heap_str_tests.rs` (9, heap level: atoms and long strings, concat, rope reads, equality of all kinds, keys, GC and byte count, 1M-deep rope in both directions, limits) and `eval_str_tests.rs` (5, JS level, expected values from Node: long strings equal by content in `===`, `includes`, `switch`, `Set`, `Map`, object keys and `Symbol.for`; a 3000-part loop; a 1M-part loop; ropes as keys and arguments; long names as keys). I wrote the tests after the code, not before.
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast` (run again at the end): the same 7 openssl failures and no other, apart from the flaky downloads test (first run: 3833 passed, 8 failed). 7 failures are in `bare-net --test https_openssl` (2), `bare-tls --test client_openssl` (4) and `bare-tls --test tls12_openssl` (1): the same groups fail on main on this machine (see the section above). 1 failure, `downloads::run::tests::a_changed_file_starts_again_from_zero`, passes when it runs alone (flaky; it does not touch strings).
- `TEST262=/data/claude-tmp/test262 tools/js/test262_check.sh`: gate ok, no directory lost a passing test (checkout at the commit of the subset). `tools/js/exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences.
- Journeys: the page console shows the same errors as base on `craigslist-home`, `go-dev-home` and `nextjs-docs`. A first build showed `InvalidKey` errors (long names were not atoms). That is fixed and covered by `eval_str_tests.rs`.

### Not tested

- Wall time on an idle machine. Peak memory of a long page that builds many ropes (only the concat loop). `ATOM_MAX` other than 32. A page that flattens a deep rope inside a regexp (`exec`) or a `JSON.parse`. Live sites.

## Standing exception: PR #497 string atoms and ropes cost (approved by owner 2026-11-14)

After two fix runs, 12 of 803 cost rows stay above +0.5% under both allocators. The worst row is +0.93%. The rows are `wrapper_load forin` (2 rows), `gen_load iterobj` (2 rows), `iterator_load` generic (2 rows), `iterator_load set_diff`, `iterator_load set_sym`, `sc_load custom_iter 10`, `tagged_load sites 10`, `weak_load dead_cycles 10` and `arrobj_load tosorted 10`. They create objects and read `for-in` keys: `new_object_with_shape` costs about 23 more instructions for each call. The matrix mean is -0.35% under glibc. keycost is +0.2%. The 47 journeys are +0.1% in total, with `python-docs-search-results` +0.7% and `python-docs-search` +0.6%. The owner approved an exception for these 12 rows only. Reason: a loop of `s += x` is now linear. 10,000 parts take 2.0 ms and 6 MiB, not 85.6 ms and 197 MiB. 100,000 and 1,000,000 parts no longer stop at the byte limit.

## P3 register VM spike (2026-11-14, `docs/design-js.md` phase P3)

Branch `t3/register-bytecode-vm-spike`. The tree walker stays the default. The lane runs with `BARE_JS_EXEC=byte` (or `auto`).

### Result: the gate passes

`eval_load CASE 10`, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, `GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=65535`, archMachine, 3 runs each (the three runs differ by under 0.01%). Numbers are the median.

| Case | Base f6415364 tree | Main f68e956a tree | Branch tree | Branch byte | Byte vs main tree |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `loopfn` | 4,091.19 M | 4,091.20 M | 4,091.20 M | 841.24 M | **4.86x** (gate 4x) |
| `fib` | 165.83 M | 166.30 M | 166.30 M | 53.52 M | **3.11x** (gate 3x) |
| `loop` (globals) | 5,015.18 M | 5,019.19 M | | 2,527.23 M | 1.99x |
| `calls` | 3,533.41 M | 3,540.41 M | | 2,116.46 M | 1.67x |
| `closures` | 669.91 M | 668.12 M | | 544.26 M | 1.23x |

- Checksums are ok in both modes on all five cases.
- The tree lane of the branch is the same as main: `loopfn` and `fib` differ by under 0.001%.
- Cost of a call of `fib`: 546 instructions in the register lane, 1,763 in tree (the difference between scale 10 and scale 1, over 84,374 calls). The first version, before `CallR`, cost 627 (`fib` 61.0 M, 2.72x: below the gate).
- Cost per op: `loopfn` runs 6 ops in an iteration (`JnLtK MulK Add ModK Inc Jmp`) for about 424 instructions, so about 71 for each op, against 46 in R1 on locals in stage 1. This is not better than R1 for each op. The gain is fewer ops (6, not 9 with 4 for `i++`) and no environment. Hypothesis: `fmod` costs a large part of the 424. I did not measure it alone.

### What was built

- Ops: fused compare-and-jump (`JnLt JnLe JnGt JnGe JnEq JnNe JnSEq JnSNe` with a register or a constant on the right), `AddK SubK MulK DivK ModK`, `CallR`. `Inc` and `Dec` from stage 1 are used in place.
- `bc_gen_rf.rs`: the generator of a register function. A function is RF when it is a plain function, arrow or method with simple parameters, no `async` or generator, no inner function, class, `with`, `arguments`, `new.target`, `super` or own name. TDZ is checked while generating, in order. A name from outside is read from the closure environment.
- `bc_vm.rs`: one loop for RF frames. A call of an RF from an RF reuses the argument registers of the caller as the registers of the callee. The call keeps `depth`, the step budget, the `Error.stack` frame, `strict` and the environment. One place unwinds an error through the frames.
- The verifier checks fused jumps, constant operands and the register layout of an RF.
- Stage 1 golden listings are unchanged: they run with the register lane off (`rf_off`). One new test, `a_simple_function_is_a_register_function`.

### Checks

- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 3,890 passed, 7 failed. The 7 are the known openssl TLS tests (`bare-net --test https_openssl` 2, `bare-tls --test client_openssl` 4, `bare-tls --test tls12_openssl` 1).
- `tools/js/exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences between tree, auto and byte.
- `tools/js/test262_check.sh` (tree): gate ok. With `BARE_JS_EXEC=byte` the gate says one directory lost tests against the baseline: `language/module-code/top-level-await` (40 to 37). The same three tests fail in byte on main (the base build f9a0c26b16 gives the same three results), so they are stage 1 faults, not new: `top-level-await/fulfillment-order`, `rejection-order` and `unobservable-global-async-evaluation-count-reset`. The byte results differ from tree in one more test, `module-code/namespace/internals/super-access-to-tdz-binding` (a different message, fails in both).
- `tools/js/cost_matrix.sh` (main f68e956a against the branch, switch off, glibc; jemalloc runs only for a row over the limit): 803 rows, 0 rows over under one allocator, 0 over under both, mean -0.004%. Two rows fail to run in both trees (`parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10`: the known stack overflow).

### What the lane does not cover

- A function with an inner function, arrow, class, `arguments`, `new.target`, `super`, `with` or its own name runs in the stage 1 lane: all its variables stay in environments.
- A `switch` with `let` or `const`, generators and async functions: stage 1 or tree.
- A call from an RF to a function that is not an RF, and `new`, go through `bc_call` and Rust recursion.
- A call from a native function (`map`, `sort`, a callback) enters the loop again by Rust recursion.
- Script bodies keep globals in cells, so `loop` gains only 1.99x.
- Module code with top-level await in the byte lane (the 3 tests above).
- Not changed: `Auto` is not the default. The GC still runs only at depth 0.

### Plan for the full stage 2

1. Boxed cells for captured variables. This makes a function with a closure an RF and lifts the largest limit (`closures` is 1.23x now).
2. `new` and inline calls of constructors; calls from RF to a stage 1 function in the same loop.
3. Global access through the cells of the script by an inline cache, to bring `loop` from 1.99x to the `loopfn` level.
4. Cost per op: profile the loop op by op (the 71 per op above), check `fmod`, the step tick of `Jmp` and the register bounds checks.
5. GC safepoints at back edges and calls (the register stack is the root set). Then `Auto` as the default only when fallbacks are 0 on the corpora.
6. Fix the 3 `top-level-await` byte tests.

### Not tested

- Wall time on an idle machine. The 48 journeys and the ramps in `/data/bare-tmp/bm` with the register lane on. A page that throws inside a deep chain of inline calls beyond the unit tests and exec_diff rows. `Error.stack` text of inline frames against Node beyond the exec_diff fixtures. Peak memory of a deep recursion (the register stack grows by `resize`). e16.
## JS compact objects: three property values inside the object record (2026-11-14, `docs/design-js.md` phase P5)

Status: pushed, not merged. The cost gate has 4 rows over +0.5% under both allocators. The memory target for `python-docs-search-results` is not met.

### What I built

An object keeps its first 3 property values inside its own record. A fourth value moves all values to one `Vec`. The 3 inline values hold the `length` of an array, the `length`, `name` and `prototype` of a function, and the properties of most object literals. An object with 3 or fewer properties needs no allocation outside the slab.

### Layout before and after

Before (80 B record): `proto`, `shape`, flags, `elems: Vec<Option<Value>>` (24 B), `slots: Vec<Value>` (24 B), `dict: Option<Box<PropMap>>` (8 B). The slab adds about 13 B for each object (`Meta` 8 B, `back` 4 B, `marks` 1 B). The values are a separate malloc block. A vector made by `push` has room for 4 values.

After (104 B record): the same fields, but `slots` becomes `repr: Repr` plus `n: u8`. `Repr` is `In([Value; 3])` or `Heap(Vec<Value>)`. They share 48 B (the compiler uses the niche of `Value`; checked with `size_of`). `n` counts the values of `In`. `dict` stays a separate field. It is `Some` exactly when the object is in dictionary mode, and then `repr` is empty.

Bytes for each object, with the slab overhead and the glibc chunk rule (usable size plus 8 B, rounded up to 16 B, at least 32 B). This is arithmetic, not a measurement:

| Object | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no property (wrapper, `{}`) | 80 + 13 = 93 B | 104 + 13 = 117 B (+24 B) |
| array with `length` only | 93 + 32 = 125 B | 117 B |
| literal with 2 properties (exact vector, 32 B) | 93 + 48 = 141 B | 117 B |
| function (3 properties, exact vector, 48 B) | 93 + 64 = 157 B | 117 B |
| 4 properties made by `push` (vector of 4 before, vector of 6 after) | 93 + 80 = 173 B | 117 + 112 = 229 B (+56 B) |

An object with no property costs 24 B more. The accounted bytes of a `Number` wrapper are now 125 B. Before, they were at most 120 B (the limit of the test `a_wrapper_costs_one_object_and_one_table_entry`; I did not measure the old value). The limit is now 128 B.

### Numbers (baseline `f6415364` was frozen; this section compares with main `f68e956a`, the base of the branch after the rebase)

All runs use the virtual clock and the recorded corpus. 3 runs each.

- 47 journeys, `tools/bench/journeys.sh compare --clock virtual --runs 3 --pss`: all 47 pass. Sum of median instructions 90,333 M to 89,721 M (-0.7%). The design expected -0.7 points: met. Spread of the same binary: 0.2% or less on 46 journeys, 2.9% on `wikipedia-search` (base).
- Peak RSS: sum 1,691.8 MiB to 1,672.3 MiB (-1.2%). `python-docs-search-results` 96.9 to 96.4 MiB (-0.5%). `rust-book-search` 131.9 to 126.7 MiB (-4.0%). `react-docs` 102.1 to 99.2 MiB (-2.9%).
- The design expected about -12 MiB (10%) on `python-docs-search-results`. I got -0.5 MiB: not met. Cause: its heap holds mostly arrays that have one value (88.7k arrays when I counted). An array with only `length` saves 8 B, not 60 B. The estimate of the design is older than the data-literal change. The design's 32 to 40 B record and size-class slabs would save more. I did not build them (see decisions).
- PSS sum went from 1,298.9 MiB to 1,317.3 MiB (+1.4%) while peak RSS went down. I did not find the cause. Hypothesis: PSS is a sample every 20 ms on a loaded machine. CPU time (+1.4%) and wall time (+1.7%) are also from a loaded machine.
- Cost matrix (`tools/js/cost_matrix.sh`, 803 rows, minimum of 3 runs, main `f68e956a` against the branch): 393 rows below -0.5%, 406 inside the band, 4 above +0.5% under both allocators. Sum of rows -0.54%. The 4 rows (glibc, jemalloc): `proxy_load keys 1` (+0.69%, +0.53%), `proxy_load keys 10` (+1.04%, +0.74%), `recursion_load react 1000` (+0.68%, +0.68%), `reflect_load keys 10` (+1.44%, +0.52%). `parse_load deep 1` and `10` fail as on main (stack overflow).
- The 12 rows of the string-atom exception (PR #497) are recovered: `gen_load iterobj` -9.0% and -9.6%, `iterator_load generic` -6.4% and -6.6%, `iterator_load set_diff` and `set_sym` -0.5% to -0.2%, `sc_load custom_iter 10` -10.0%, `tagged_load sites 10` -1.0%, `weak_load dead_cycles 10` -11.0%, `wrapper_load forin` -1.7% and -1.3%, `arrobj_load tosorted 10` 0.0%. I did not measure the instructions of one `new_object_with_shape` call. The 12 rows moved because an object literal now fills inline values and makes no vector.
- Keycost (`tools/js/typing/keycost.sh`): `#a1` 294.8 to 295.7 M for each key (+0.3%), `#f0` 300.1 to 301.1 M (+0.3%). Load and mount 620.0 M to 613.8 M (-1.0%). Peak RSS at 50 keys 34.3 to 30.7 MiB.

### What went wrong on the way

- A first matrix had 52 rows over +0.5%, up to +10% (`date_load clock`, `web_apis_load base64`, `proxy_load` +7%), and `react-docs` failed (`Object.keys is not a function` after the second page). Cause: `Object::to_shapes` did not clear `dict`, so an object that left dictionary mode kept a stale dictionary and was read as dictionary mode by part of the code. Three tests of `bare-js` failed and showed it. The commit "Drop the dictionary when an object returns to shape mode" fixes it, with the test `leaving_dictionary_mode_drops_the_dictionary_and_keeps_the_values`. I had run only a filtered test set before (`heap`), which hid the failures.
- My cost analysis of the earlier variants (a 3-way `Repr` with `Dict(Box<PropMap>)`, 96 B) was made before I found this bug. The bug exists only in the 2-way layout, so the numbers of the 3-way variant are not affected by it. I could not separate the effect of the 3-way layout from other causes in the time I had. I kept the 2-way layout with a separate `dict` field, the one that I measured last. I did not show that it is better than the 3-way layout.
- One more change did not help: a single `n != 0` test for `has_slots`. `proxy_load keys` improved, but `reflect_load keys` went from +1.4% to +2.6% and `arrobj_load freeze`, `lastindexof` and `date_load cap` went over +0.5%. I reverted it. Instruction counts do not depend on load, so the changes come from inlining and code layout. Hypothesis: the 4 remaining rows are the same effect (a few more instructions in `has_property` and `shape_get`: callgrind on `proxy_load keys 1` shows `has_property` +240 k, `shape_get` +165 k of 55.9 M).

### Checks

- `cargo test --release -p bare-js`: 947 tests pass.
- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: the 7 known openssl TLS failures and the known `a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved` failure. No other failure.
- `TEST262=/data/claude-tmp/test262 tools/js/test262_check.sh`: exit 0, no directory lost a passing test (it lists directories that gained tests since the stored baseline; they come from main).
- `tools/js/exec_diff.sh`: 79 runs, 0 differences.
- New tests: values stay readable across the inline limit and after deletes; array `length` and named properties; leaving dictionary mode drops the dictionary.

### Not tested

- The JS ramps of the benchmark round and the `bare-bench` JS rows.
- Wall time on an idle machine.
- The peak memory of an object-heavy page other than the three named journeys.
- The 8-byte `Value`, `proto` stored in the shape, JSON objects with shapes, and the design's size-class slabs. None of them is built.

## Rule-set sharing, stage 1: process-wide atoms and a rule-set cache (2026-11-14)

Task: build stage 1 of `docs/design-rule-share.md`. Branch `t3/rule-set-cache`, rebased on main `f6292d53`. Stage 2 (a parse cache for each sheet) is not built.

Owner decision (2026-11-14): build stage 1 of the design, in this order. First, atoms that all documents of a thread share. Measure `intern` and the change on the cost matrix before the cache, and fix by design if the cost rule breaks. Second, an `Rc<RuleSet>` cache keyed by the ordered sheet list and the window size.

### What I built

- Atoms (`crates/html/src/dom.rs`). One name table for each thread. An `Atom` has the same number in every document of the thread. A document keeps the list and the bit map of the names that it uses, so `name_count`, `atom_at`, `find_atom` and `new_names_in` keep their meaning, and the name cap of a document still counts its own names.
- Rule-set cache (`crates/css/src/rule_cache.rs`). A set is shared when the list has no shadow-tree sheet, no retained CSSOM input and no pending inline input. The key is a hash of the window size, and of the layer and text of each sheet. A hit compares the layers, the window size and all the texts, so a hash collision is a miss (`RuleSet::built_from`). A page that appends a sheet grows its own set in place when the cache and the page are the only holders (`unshare`). Otherwise it builds the set again.
- What is shared, and why it is safe. `decls`, `side`, `customs`, `reach`, `Index::big`, the lazy bodies, `logical` and `motion` are made from the rules alone, only grow, and no borrow of them overlaps with another (one thread, no re-entry). `tested` and `styled` are read as differences around one call. I use `Rc`, not `Arc`: a set never leaves its thread.
- What bounds the cache. At most `MAX_RULES` (65,536) rules in sets that only the cache holds. I measured 500 to 620 bytes for each rule with unread bodies (1,000 rules: 1.47 MB, 20,000: 12.4 MB, 65,000: 32.9 MB), so the bound is about 33 MB in the worst case. An entry that none of the last 2 documents used goes when a document starts (`Browser::new`). A document keeps its own set in any case. Of the sets that one document used, only the last one stays: a page that changes its sheets while it loads builds one set for each list, and the sets before the last are in no other page (this was the first cause of extra memory, see "Memory").

### Findings during the build

- The cost rule broke at step 1: +3.3% on large `bare-stress` pages, 180 rows over under both allocators. A thread-local table with a `RefCell` on each `atom_str` and `intern` cost that. The fix was by design: each document keeps a `&'static` reference to the table, a read of a name text uses an `UnsafeCell` and no flag, the first use of a name in a document is a cold function, and the hash is a word hash. At the cache step the cost matrix still had 12 rows over (about +0.6%: `intern` of each tag name costs about 100 instructions, 20,000 elements). A front table of 512 slots for names of 8 bytes or less removed the hash, the probe and the compare for almost every tag and attribute: `boxes-one-long-run 20000` went from +0.57% to -0.68% against main (callgrind).
- A hidden dependency on the sheet of the browser (a real bug that the cache exposed). `Hints::new` gave `None` when no `table` atom was in the document. Each document had that atom, because the sheet of the browser has a `table` selector. On a cache hit that sheet is not read, so an `<img width=30 height=40>` lost its size (`rects_cases` failed: 5 of 54 cases). `Hints::new` now looks for each tag that has a hint. The unit test that described the old behavior (an `<img>` page with no table has no hint) now says the browser always hinted an `img`.
- A race in the driver that the cache made visible. The `write` tests of the suite failed in 1% to 14% of the runs (`type` on `#note`: "did not take the focus after the click"), and 3 of 8 suite runs failed. Cause: `Page::click` moves the pointer, the move lets the page run, a `fetch` fills a list, the input moves down, and the button goes down on the old place. The network log of a failing run shows the reply at 35.0 ms inside step 12. Main has the same race, but a rule-set build that takes 3 ms hid it. With the cache off in the same binary (`BARE_NO_SHARE`, a temporary switch that is not in the code): 0 of 400 failed; with it on: 57 of 400. Fix (in `control.rs`): after the move, when the element is not under the pointer, aim again with `actionable`. The hit test that checks this is the one that the button makes next, so it costs no instructions. A version that always aimed again cost +240 M on the suite. Test: `a_click_aims_again_after_the_page_moved_the_element` (it fails without the fix). After the fix: 0 of 400 cold runs of `36-write-3` and of `34-write-1`, and 12 of 12 suite runs pass. `dblclick` and `hover` have the same pattern. I did not change them.

### Numbers

Machine archMachine, 16 cores, shared (load 3 to 14 while I measured). Instruction counts are stable. 3 runs each unless I say so.

| Measure | Frozen `f6415364` | Main `f68e956a` | Branch (final) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Suite, 40 tests, 1 worker, shared login (V2), M instructions | not measured (V0, a new process for each test: 21,078, spread 21,064 to 21,134) | 13,147 (13,110 to 13,163). V0: 18,239 | 10,431 (10,414 to 10,432). V0: 15,542. -20.7% against main V2; 2.02 times lower than the frozen V0 |
| Suite of 800 tests (the 40 repeated 20 times), V2, 1 run, M instructions | | 258,127, peak RSS of the worker 28.06 MiB | 205,325 (-20.5%), 28.60 MiB (+0.54 MiB) |
| 47 journeys, virtual clock, sum of medians, M instructions | 105,217 (from `perf-goal.md`) | 90,534 | 90,293 (-0.3%) |
| 47 journeys, sum of peak RSS | | 1,691 MiB | 1,730 MiB (+2.3%). PSS 1,448 / 1,483 MiB (+2.5%) |
| `compm_22000`, M instructions | 11,664 (spread 0.001%) | 1,834 | 1,829 |
| `rest_13`, M instructions | 10,873 | 1,241 | 1,239 |
| Keycost, `#a1` and `#f0`, M for each key | | 294.77, 300.13 | 294.76, 300.12 |

- The design expected 13.1 G to about 10.75 G on the suite. The result is 10.43 G: a build costs 11.2 M and the suite makes 190 of them.
- Journeys: one process, mostly different sites, so a hit is rare. Gains: `docs-rs-home` -23.7%, `duckduckgo-html-search` -16.3%, `rust-lang-org-home` -12.8%, `python-docs-tutorial` -4.9%, `python-org-docs-link` and `python-org-search` -2.8% (a repeated sheet list). All the other journeys are within 0.5%. `python-docs-search-results`: instructions -1.2%, peak RSS +0.1%, so criterion 6 does not move. Criterion 3 does not move either, as the design said: each ramp is one document, so the first build is a miss. Criterion 7 (instructions with one worker, target 1.5 times lower): 2.02 times against the frozen V0. Against the V0 of the same binary: 1.49 times.
- Cost matrix (`tools/js/cost_matrix.sh`, 803 rows, against main `f68e956a`, base counts cached): 0 rows over +0.5% under both allocators, 0 under one. Mean change glibc -0.23%. `parse_load deep 1` and `deep 10` fail to run (stack overflow) on main too.

### Memory (the cost of the cache)

- Before the last two changes the 47 journeys gave peak RSS +4.3% and `wikipedia-article` +26%: the cache kept every set of a page that changes its sheets while it loads (Wikipedia: four lists, python.org: three), so up to six sets were in memory together.
- Tried and dropped: drop all the sets that only the cache holds at each miss. Memory +3%, but the instruction gain of the repeated lists was gone (`python-org-*` -8% to 0%): a page builds three lists, and the second document would have hit all three.
- Kept: the sets of one document go when the document goes on to another list, and when a document starts only its last set stays (`use_key`, `drop_step`).
- Result: the Wikipedia journeys +4% to +14% peak RSS (+2.5 to +6.4 MiB), `github-docs-home` +8%, `wiktionary-portal` +8%, `python-org-*` +11%. This is one set of the page before, which the next document may hit. A journey that visits only new sites pays for it and gets nothing back. A suite that returns to one site gets the 20%. I did not find a rule that tells these two apart before the next document asks. The owner decides if the memory is worth it.

### Checks

- `cargo test --release --workspace --no-fail-fast`: see the last line of this section.
- New tests: `crates/html` (short names, two documents share atoms), `crates/css` (`rule_cache`: 6 tests; the cross-document differential in `cascade/index_tests.rs`), `crates/bare/src/browser_rule_share_tests.rs` (11: same sheets, window size, CSSOM edit, inserted style, grown set, late link, layered part, shadow tree, retained inputs, image hint, with and without the cache give the same styles), `control_tests.rs` (the click). The differential test fails on the commit before the global atoms.
- Failures that are not mine. On a run of the workspace: `bare-net --test https_openssl` (2) and `bare-tls` `client_openssl` (4) and `tls12_openssl` (1) fail with `BadSignature` in the test certificates; these crates do not depend on html or css. `downloads::run::tests::a_changed_file_starts_again_from_zero` and `bare-mcp --test server a_hidden_iframe_download_is_saved` are flaky: the second counts "(0 bytes)" of a download that is still running, and passes one run in three. Run alone, the first passes.
- Not run: `test262_check.sh` and `exec_diff.sh` (`crates/js` is not touched).

### Not tested

- Wall time on an idle machine (the suite wall time here is from a loaded machine). Live sites. A page with many frames (each frame is a document of the thread: `new_document` ages the cache for it too). A suite on more than one worker (the cache is for each thread, so each worker builds its own sets). `dblclick` and `hover` with a page that moves under the pointer. The peak RSS of a long run on a site with a very large sheet (the 65,536-rule bound is from the measured bytes for each rule, not from a run that reaches it).

### Noticed, not changed

- The global name table only grows. A document is capped by `max_names`, the table is not. A thread that opens many different sites collects every tag and attribute name of them. I measured no problem on the suite or the journeys. An epoch or a reset when the cache and all documents are gone would bound it.
- `name_count` of a document can differ between a cache hit and a miss: selector parsing interns names into the document that builds the set.
- `dblclick` and `hover` aim once, like `click` did.

## P3 register VM, stage 2 slice 1: closures, inline calls and global cells (2026-11-14, `docs/design-js.md` phase P3)

Branch `t3/bytecode-closures-globals`, rebased on main `1e793d74`. The tree walker stays the default. The lane runs with `BARE_JS_EXEC=byte` or `auto`. The browser session now reads `BARE_JS_EXEC` too (`SessionConfig::new`), so the journeys can run the lane. With the variable unset the mode is `Tree`, as before.

### What I built

1. Captured variables (a function with inner functions is a register function with an environment). The call makes the stage 1 environment (`new_env` and `bind_call`). A variable that an inner function names stays a binding of that environment. All other variables are registers. A scope has a run-time environment only when an inner function lies inside it, so the hop count of `bc_resolve` stays right for the inner function, on the tree walker and in the lane. Boxed cells of a new kind were not needed: the existing `Env` layout is the cell.
2. Inline calls. A call from any lane code (stage 1, register function, register function with environment) to any compiled function of the same script runs in the same loop, with no Rust frame. A frame keeps its own environment depth (`Fr.depth`) and the environment of its call (`Fr.callee_env`). `bc_frame_exit` unwinds them. Default parameter values run in the callee environment and frame.
3. Global cells. A cell keeps the position of a global property, or the index of a binding of environment 0, with the count of those bindings. Environment 0 only gains bindings, so a cell stays valid while the count is the same. A script with `let`, `const` or `class` at top level (environment 0 not empty) uses the cell too.
4. Counters: `BARE_JS_STATS=1` prints, for each interpreter, the functions compiled, the calls that the lane ran, the calls that the tree walker ran because the lane refused the function, and the refusal reasons.

Order. The plan puts boxed cells first, then calls, then global cells. The task listed globals first. I followed the plan: a global cell gains nothing while environment 0 is empty (the `loop` row did not move), and the gain of a closure is larger (`closures` 1.23x to 1.35x, and every function with an inner function stops being stage 1).

Not built: inline `new`. `new` goes through `bc_call` and `construct` (Rust recursion). A call from a native function (`map`, `sort`, a callback) enters the loop again by Rust recursion. Both work and are covered by the differential tests.

### Numbers: `eval_load CASE 10`

`tools/js/instr.sh` method (`instructions:u`, large malloc cache), archMachine, 3 runs each, the three runs differ by under 0.01%. Tree is the same on main and on the branch (under 0.01%). "Main byte" is main `1e793d74` with `BARE_JS_EXEC=byte`.

| Case | Tree | Main byte | Branch byte | Tree / branch byte |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `loopfn` | 4,091.0 M | 841.0 M | 823.0 M | 4.97x |
| `fib` | 165.9 M | 53.2 M | 56.6 M | 2.93x |
| `loop` (globals) | 5,007.0 M | 2,515.0 M | 2,487.0 M | 2.01x |
| `calls` | 3,532.2 M | 2,109.3 M | 1,641.3 M | 2.15x |
| `closures` | 646.4 M | 522.5 M | 478.8 M | 1.35x |
| `objects` | 2,389.4 M | 2,329.0 M | 2,335.8 M | 1.02x |
| `throws` | 1,947.2 M | 1,496.2 M | 1,490.5 M | 1.31x |
| `webpack` | 38.5 M | 50.2 M | 50.5 M | 0.76x |

- `fib` costs 6.3% more than on main in the lane: 581 instructions for each call, against 546. The cause is the larger frame record and the two checks of the environment of a frame. I made `bc_frame_exit` inline (60.4 M to 56.6 M). A cold side for the environments made it worse (58.4 M), because of code layout, so I kept the first form. The spike gate of 3x on `fib` is now 2.93x.
- `webpack` is slower in the lane than in the tree walker: 502 functions compile, and each runs about 3 times. This is the compile cost. `auto` gives the same number as `byte`, because it compiles at the second call. A start of the lane in `byte` mode costs 0.3 M instructions more than on main (`fib 1`: 7.20 M to 7.50 M).
- `loop` is limited by the script body, not by globals. The body of a script runs as stage 1 (a stack code), about 600 instructions for each iteration. `loopfn` is 410.

### Numbers: ramps and journeys

- JS ramps of the benchmark round (`/data/bare-tmp/bm/b/pages`, `bare-drive`, 3 runs, spread under 0.01%). `steps_1000000` (a loop in a script body): tree 1,812.5 M, lane 959.5 M (1.89x). `steps_10000000`: 18,057.5 M and 9,527.5 M (1.90x). `nest_100`: 7.7 M and 7.9 M. `nest_1022`: 10.7 M and 11.0 M (+2.8%: the compile cost of the first call is not paid back). All pass in both modes.
- 47 journeys on the recorded virtual-clock corpus, lane on against off (`/data/bare-tmp/slice1/jrun.py`, 3 runs each, spread 0.4% or less): the sum of instructions goes from 89,935 M to 89,871 M (-0.07%), median row -0.08%. No journey is over +5%. The best rows: `crates-io-home` -48.4% (132 M to 68 M), `docs-rs-home` -22.6%, `duckduckgo-html-search` -16.5%, `rust-lang-org-home` -12.3%. The worst: `rust-book-sidebar` +2.8%, `nodejs-org-home` +2.3%, `rust-book-chapters` +2.1%. PSS sum 1,315 MiB to 1,320 MiB (+0.4%). PSS is a poll every 20 ms in the first run only, so single rows (for example -99% on `crates-io-home`) are noise. `nextjs-docs` fails in both modes (it is flaky on main too).
- **The lane runs 34.9% of the function calls of the 47 journeys** (1,090 k of 3,127 k). The tree walker runs the other 65.1% after the lane refused the function. The reasons, in calls: `no scope` 1,629 k (80% of the refused calls: the body of a lazy function, which the lane never runs), `wide form` 276 k (13.5%), `destructuring` 65 k, `spread` 39 k, `for-in or for-of` 17 k, `regexp literal` 6 k.
- Answer for the owner: the lane is not ready to become the default. On the journeys it gives -0.07% instructions and +0.4% memory. The cost of compiling is paid by cold pages, and the gain is on the pages that run a hot loop in a function. Two designs move the share: run lazy bodies in the lane (80% of the refused calls), and compile the script body as a register function (the `steps` ramps and `loop`).

### What went wrong on the way

- A first journey run showed -10% instructions in total, with `react-docs` -55% and `mdn-reference` -24%. It was wrong: `function f(a, b = a + 1)` and `function f(a, ...r)` failed in the lane ("a binding that the code generator expected"), because a call from the loop evaluated the default values before the callee environment was current. The page swallowed the error and ran less code. A journey that passes only shows that its steps pass, not that the JS result is the same. `exec_diff.sh` found it (2 differences). With the fix `react-docs` is -2% and `mdn-reference` +0.9%.
- The same run showed `go-dev-home` at 46.3 G instead of 3.2 G. Cause: `bc_resolve` built the list of bindings of a scope for each site of a function, so a function with many sites in a large scope cost sites times statements. The list is now the cached template of the scope (`bc_tmpl`). The old code is on main and runs in `byte` mode there too. I did not run main on the journeys: main ignores the switch in the browser.
- `local_at` found a variable of an outer scope when a captured variable of an inner scope had the same name (`var x; { let x; { const x; return (() => x)() } }`). A captured name now stops the search.

## Rule-set cache: idle sets bounded by bytes (2026-11-14)

Task: stage 1 of rule-set sharing (#515) raised the summed peak RSS of the 47 journeys by 2.3% (1,691 to 1,730 MiB), and the Wikipedia journeys by 4% to 14%. The cause was the last set of the document before, kept in the cache. Branch `t3/bound-rule-cache-bytes`, rebased on main `8d64702a`.

Owner decision (2026-11-14): bound the idle sets (sets that only the cache holds) by bytes. Keep small repeated lists, drop large one-off sets. Compare at least two eviction rules before choosing one. Target: journeys summed peak RSS within +0.5% of the build before #515 (1,691 MiB), Wikipedia journeys within +1%, most of the instruction gain on `docs-rs-home`, `duckduckgo-html-search`, `rust-lang-org-home`, and the suite at about 10.4 G.

### What I built

- `RuleSet::heap_bytes` (`cascade.rs`, `Selector::heap_bytes` in `selector.rs`): the live bytes of a set, counted from the sizes of its tables, also the lazily read blocks and the split lists.
- `rule_cache`: idle sets weigh at most `MAX_IDLE_BYTES` = 2,500,000. Over that, the set with the lowest priority goes. Priority = uses + the priority of the last set that went (GDSF with a cost in proportion to the size, so uses and age decide).
- `settle` (called by the document after it replaced its set): the step of a page (the set before its next one) goes at once. Before, it went one list too late, so each loading page held one set more than before #515.
- `Cache::diverged`: a document that asks for a list that the document before it did not ask for is on another site. The idle sets that it did not use go at that look. A page of the same site makes the same lists in the same order.
- `MAX_RULES` (65,536 rules) is removed. The real bound is now the bytes. The `max_rules` and `max_names` limits of a document stay.

### Measurement 1: the live size of a set (bytes, not rules)

A counting allocator in a temporary build (not committed: `/data/bare-tmp/rcb/experiment-all.patch`) measured the bytes that one build leaves alive, for the first build of each of the 45 journeys that build one. `heap_bytes` gives 0.90 to 1.00 of that (the difference is the allocator's own bookkeeping of the sheet of the browser, about 7 KB, so small sets are the 0.90). Sets with 400 or more rules are 0.95 to 1.00.

| Set | Rules | Live bytes | Bytes for each rule |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| suite fixture (60 KB sheet) | 2,272 | 1.31 MB | 577 |
| `docs-rs-home` | 1,333 | 0.94 MB | 704 |
| `duckduckgo-html-search` | 1,489 | 0.97 MB | 648 |
| `rust-lang-org-home` | 2,201 | 1.19 MB | 542 |
| `wikipedia-article`, last list | 1,782 to 2,533 | 1.31 to 2.06 MB | 734 to 813 |
| `python-org-docs-link`, the list that hits | 2,938 | 2.19 MB (2.26 MB after styles read blocks) | 745 |
| `github-docs-home` | 8,919 | 7.88 MB | 884 |
| `devto-home` | 17,456 | 12.4 MB | 711 |

The sets that a later document found in the cache (31 hits in 22 journeys) are 0.08 to 2.26 MB. The sets that were idle and never hit (18 cases) sum to 19 MB, 7.9 MB of that is `github-docs-home`. A hit set and a wasted set have the same sizes, so size alone cannot tell them apart. All hits are one document after the set was used.

### Measurement 2: the rules

Journeys: `journeys.sh compare --clock virtual`, corpus `virtual`, 47 journeys. Base is main before #515 (`f68e956a`). The same-binary spread of the sum is -0.30% to +0.16% for RSS and -0.4% to -0.1% for the Wikipedia rows (two runs of 5, the binary against itself). Peak heap is the peak of live bytes of the page thread (counting allocator, deterministic: two runs gave the same number).

| Config | RSS sum, median / min | Wikipedia RSS, median / min | Instructions | Peak heap sum (Wikipedia) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| #515 as merged (15 runs) | +1.25% / +1.26% | +3.7% / +4.3% | -0.76% | 775.2 MiB (145.1) |
| drop every idle set at each look (9 runs) | -0.51% | +1.2% (noise) | -0.64%, gains of the 3 journeys gone (-2.0%, -1.7%, -1.7%) | 763.5 (143.7) |
| `settle` and 2.5 MB, no `diverged` (15 runs) | +0.66% / +0.41% | +2.0% / +2.4% | -0.74% | 765.4 (144.0) |
| `settle`, 2.5 MB and `diverged` (15 runs) | +0.26% / -0.20% | +0.2% / +0.1% | -0.74% | 764.1 (143.7) |

- Byte bound alone: 1.5 MB gave +2.2% on Wikipedia (5 runs, before `settle`), 1.0 MB lost the gain of `rust-lang-org-home`, 2.5 MB gave +2.0% to +2.4%. The idle set that remains is a set of the page before that the next page does not use, and it is the same size as a set that is used. So the byte bound caps the worst case (`github-docs-home` 7.9 MB, `devto-home` 12.4 MB, `substack-home` 6.8 MB never stay), and `diverged` removes the rest.
- `settle` alone changes the peak heap by 0.3 MiB over 47 journeys (774.9 against 775.2): the step costs less than it seemed. It stays because it is the same set one list too early.
- Eviction rules among the idle sets, at 2.5 MB with `settle`: largest first, oldest first, GDSF. On the 47 journeys the peak heap is 765.4 MiB for all three: at most one or two sets are idle, so they choose the same set. On the suite the same: one set. A synthetic stream (30 sites, sizes lognormal with a median of 0.8 MB and a long tail to 8 MB, Zipf visits, half of the visits repeat the last site, 20 streams of 4,000 visits, `/data/bare-tmp/rcb/sim.py`) at 2.5 MB: hit bytes 0.580 (largest first, mean idle 2.21 MB), 0.609 (oldest first, 1.54 MB), 0.657 (GDSF, 1.83 MB). At 5 MB: 0.628, 0.672, 0.723. GDSF is chosen: the most hits at each budget, and it keeps a set that is used often.
- The number 2.5 MB: the largest set that a journey found in the cache is 2.26 MB (`python-org-docs-link`); 2.5 MB leaves 0.24 MB of room over it. The suite's set is 1.37 MB. Below 2.3 MB the `python-org-*` gain (-3.2%) is lost.

Journeys, 9 runs, base = main before #515 (`f68e956a`):

| Measure | Before #515 | Branch |

| Peak RSS, sum of medians | 1,684.0 MiB | 1,681.6 MiB (-0.14%). Minimum of the runs: 1,659.6 / 1,658.0 (-0.09%) |

Against main with #515 (`1e793d74`), 9 runs: instructions 89,713 M to 89,727 M (+0.02%), peak RSS 1,707.9 to 1,688.0 MiB (-1.2%), Wikipedia -3.3% to -9.8% for each journey (-4.9% summed). `github-docs-home` -7.7%, `python-org-docs-link` -4.4%. The three gains stay (+0.2% to +0.4% against #515 on those rows, 0.2 to 0.3 M).

Suite (40 tests, one worker, shared login, 3 runs): branch 10,053 M (10,042 to 10,067), main with #515 10,061 M (10,054 to 10,066), before #515 13,162 M. Peak RSS of the worker 27.1 (26.8 to 27.4) / 26.8 / 26.2 MiB. The first build of this change walked the set at each idle check and cost 10,118 M (+0.57%); the walk now runs once for each set. Against the frozen V0 (21,078 M) the suite is 2.10 times lower. It is 10.05 G, not 10.4 G: main moved since #515.
Suite of 800 tests (the 40 repeated 20 times, `/data/bare-tmp/rcb/suite800`), 1 run: 198,211 M, 28.0 MiB; main with #515 197,976 M, 27.9 MiB; before #515 259,671 M, 27.1 MiB.

- `cargo test --release -p bare-css --lib rule_cache`: 10 tests, 4 new (`idle_sets_weigh_at_most_the_budget_and_the_one_with_fewer_uses_goes`, `a_set_over_the_budget_goes_when_nobody_holds_it`, `the_step_of_a_page_goes_when_the_page_has_its_next_set`, `a_page_on_other_lists_than_the_page_before_drops_its_idle_sets`).
